cards.counter: Historians (e.g. Andreas Osiander) argue the 'Westphalian myth' is a 19th-century back-projection; the treaties didn't actually establish modern sovereignty as commonly claimed.

cards.title: The Thucydides Trap
cards.fact: When a rising power threatens a ruling one, the result is often war.
cards.detail: Graham Allison studied 16 cases over 500 years and found war in 12. Named after Thucydides' line that it was the rise of Athens, and the fear it caused in Sparta, that made war inevitable. Applied today to the US and China.
cards.deploy: A structured frame for great-power-rivalry arguments — names the mechanism (fear of a shifting balance).
cards.counter: The case selection and what counts as a 'rise' or 'war' are contested; 'often' is not 'inevitable', and 4 of 16 avoided war.

cards.title: Chokepoint: the Strait of Hormuz
cards.fact: Roughly a fifth of the world's oil passes through one narrow strait.
cards.detail: About 20–21 million barrels a day move through the Strait of Hormuz between the Persian Gulf and open ocean — a single point of geographic leverage.
cards.deploy: Physical geography concentrates strategic power — concrete grounding for arguments about energy security.
cards.counter: Shares and volumes shift; new pipelines and changing demand steadily reduce any one chokepoint's leverage.

cards.title: Mackinder's Heartland theory (1904)
cards.fact: Whoever controls the Eurasian 'Heartland' could dominate the world — a classic land-power doctrine.
cards.detail: Halford Mackinder argued that control of inner Eurasia (the 'World-Island') was the key to global power, because it was beyond the reach of sea power.
cards.deploy: The founding lens of geopolitical 'land power vs sea power' thinking — still echoed in analyses of Russia and Central Asia.
cards.counter: Airpower, nuclear weapons, and globalised trade undercut pure land-centric determinism; geography constrains but doesn't dictate.

cards.title: Rimland: the reply to Heartland
cards.fact: The rival to Heartland theory: control the coastal 'rim' of Eurasia, not its core.
cards.detail: Nicholas Spykman (1940s) inverted Mackinder: power lies not in the inaccessible Eurasian Heartland but in the 'Rimland' — the densely populated coastal fringe (Europe, the Middle East, South and East Asia). 'Who controls the Rimland rules Eurasia.' It shaped US Cold War containment, which ringed the Soviet and Chinese landmass with alliances and bases.
cards.deploy: Decodes US grand strategy: containment and the alliance network around Eurasia's rim are Rimland thinking in action.
cards.counter: Like Heartland, it's a sweeping doctrine, not a law — air power, nuclear weapons and economics complicate any neat geography-determines-power story.

quiz.q: Spykman's Rimland theory says power lies in…

cards.title: The security dilemma
cards.fact: Arming to feel safer can make everyone less safe — the 'security dilemma'.
cards.detail: Even with no aggressive intent, one state's defensive build-up looks threatening to others, who arm in response, leaving all less secure — a spiral driven by fear and uncertainty about intentions (Herz, 1950; Jervis). It's a core reason rising-power tensions (the Thucydides Trap) can escalate without anyone actually wanting war.
cards.deploy: Explains how war can come from fear, not aggression — and why signalling restraint and intentions matters so much.
cards.counter: It's not inevitable: arms control, transparency, and clearly non-threatening 'defensive' postures can defuse the spiral; not every build-up is misread.

quiz.q: The 'security dilemma' is when…
choices: Defensive arming makes others feel threatened, spiralling insecurity

cards.title: The Malacca dilemma
cards.fact: Most of East Asia's oil squeezes through one narrow strait — the 'Malacca dilemma'.
cards.detail: The Strait of Malacca, between Malaysia and Indonesia, is the world's busiest — around 80% of China's imported crude passes through it, plus much of Japan's and Korea's trade. China's reliance on a single chokepoint a rival navy could blockade is its 'Malacca dilemma' (Hu Jintao's term, 2003), and a driver of overland pipelines, a bigger navy and the Belt and Road.
cards.deploy: A concrete lens on China's strategy: much of its energy security hangs on a strait it doesn't control.
cards.counter: A blockade would be an act of war with huge costs to all sides, so the vulnerability is more strategic anxiety than likely event — and alternatives (pipelines, reserves) are being built.

quiz.q: The 'Malacca dilemma' refers to…
choices: East Asia's reliance on one strait for oil and trade

cards.title: When populations shrink
cards.fact: The demographic transition's final twist: much of the world is now ageing and shrinking.
cards.detail: Past the transition, fertility in many countries has fallen below replacement (~2.1). Japan, South Korea, much of Europe and now China face ageing and then shrinking populations — fewer workers supporting more retirees, strained pensions and slower growth. South Korea's fertility (~0.7) is the world's lowest. Migration can offset it but is politically fraught.
cards.deploy: Reframes the population debate: for a growing share of the world the worry is too few people, not too many.
cards.counter: It's uneven — much of sub-Saharan Africa is still growing fast — and forecasts are uncertain; policy, migration and changing norms could shift fertility.

quiz.q: Below-replacement fertility leads to…

cards.title: The demographic transition
cards.fact: As countries develop, they shift from high birth-and-death rates to low — then they age.
cards.detail: Falling child mortality and development first cause a population boom, then birth rates fall and the population stabilises and greys, raising the ratio of retirees to workers.
cards.deploy: Explains why growth slows and why ageing (China, Japan, Europe) reshapes economies and pensions.
cards.counter: Trajectories vary widely; immigration, policy, and culture can speed up, slow down, or reverse parts of the transition.

cards.title: Natural selection
cards.fact: Heritable variation plus differential survival produces design without a designer.
cards.detail: Darwin (1859): organisms vary, some variations are inherited, and those that aid survival and reproduction become more common over generations — yielding apparent design.
cards.deploy: Complexity can arise from blind, cumulative processes — the canonical answer to 'it looks designed, so it was designed'.
cards.counter: Selection is one mechanism among several. Genetic drift, gene flow, and sheer contingency also shape evolution; not every trait is an adaptation.

quiz.q: Natural selection requires variation that is…

cards.title: You're about half bacteria (by cell count)
cards.fact: Your body holds roughly as many bacterial cells as human cells — about 1:1, not the old '10:1'.
cards.detail: A 2016 re-estimate put it near 38 trillion bacteria to 30 trillion human cells. The widely-repeated '10 times more bacteria than your own cells' was never well-founded.
cards.deploy: Doubles as a fact and a myth-correction — a clean way to show how a 'known' figure can be wrong.
cards.counter: These are estimates with wide ranges and they vary person to person; function matters more than raw counts.

cards.title: CRISPR: programmable gene editing
cards.fact: Since 2012 we've been able to cut and edit DNA at a chosen spot, cheaply and precisely.
cards.detail: Doudna and Charpentier showed the bacterial CRISPR-Cas9 system can be guided by a custom RNA to cut DNA wherever you point it (Nobel Prize 2020). It transformed biotech almost overnight.
cards.deploy: Cheap, precise editing changes every debate about medicine, agriculture, and 'designer' organisms.
cards.counter: Off-target edits and the ethics of heritable (germline) changes remain serious, unresolved caveats.

cards.title: Evolution by pure chance
cards.fact: Evolution isn't only survival of the fittest — pure chance ('genetic drift') also shapes which genes survive.
cards.detail: Beyond selection, gene frequencies wander randomly across generations through sheer sampling luck — who happens to reproduce. This 'genetic drift' is strongest in small populations, where it can fix or erase a gene regardless of fitness, and (per Kimura's neutral theory) it drives much molecular evolution. Selection and drift act together, not in opposition.
cards.deploy: Corrects the 'everything is an adaptation' reflex — much genetic change is just noise, not design.
cards.counter: Drift and selection are partners, not rivals; their relative weight depends on population size, and teasing them apart is genuinely hard.

quiz.q: Genetic drift changes gene frequencies through…
choices: Random chance, especially in small populations

cards.title: What your microbes do for you
cards.fact: Your resident microbes earn their keep — digesting fibre, making vitamins and training your immune system.
cards.detail: Gut microbes ferment dietary fibre into short-chain fatty acids, help synthesise vitamins (K and several B's), and help calibrate the immune system, while crowding out invaders. Disruption ('dysbiosis') — e.g. from broad-spectrum antibiotics — is associated with conditions from inflammatory bowel disease to metabolic problems, though much of the 'gut–brain' story is still emerging.
cards.deploy: Reframes microbes as partners, not passengers — and explains why broad antibiotics have side effects.
cards.counter: The field is hot and over-hyped: many microbiome–disease links are correlations, and popular 'gut–brain axis' claims often run ahead of the evidence.

quiz.q: A well-supported role of the gut microbiome is…
choices: Digesting fibre and training the immune system

cards.title: The gene-edited babies line
cards.fact: In 2018 a scientist edited the genes of babies — crossing a line the field had agreed not to.
cards.detail: CRISPR can edit body cells (somatic) to treat one patient, or the germline (eggs, sperm, embryos), whose changes pass to all descendants. In 2018 He Jiankui announced gene-edited twins in China; the work drew near-universal condemnation and a prison sentence — it was unsafe, the consent forged, the ethics indefensible. Most countries ban heritable germline editing while allowing somatic gene therapies.
cards.deploy: Marks the bright line in gene editing: treating a patient vs. permanently altering the human lineage.
cards.counter: The line is contested at the edges — a 2017 US National Academies report cautiously allowed heritable editing in principle for serious disease, so 'never' isn't a settled consensus.

quiz.q: The 2018 He Jiankui case involved editing…

cards.title: Wolves reshaped Yellowstone
cards.fact: Reintroducing wolves in 1995 rippled all the way down to the rivers.
cards.detail: With wolves back, elk grazed differently, letting willow and aspen recover, which helped beavers and stabilised some streambanks — a 'trophic cascade' from a top predator.
cards.deploy: Top predators have outsized, system-wide effects — a memorable case that removing one species isn't a local change.
cards.counter: The popular 'wolves changed the rivers' story is partly overstated; recovery had multiple drivers and the magnitude is debated.

cards.title: Planetary boundaries
cards.fact: Scientists have mapped nine limits for a stable planet — and we've crossed several.
cards.detail: The framework defines a 'safe operating space' across climate, biodiversity, the nitrogen and phosphorus cycles, freshwater, land use, and more. A 2023 update found six of nine boundaries transgressed.
cards.deploy: Moves environmental debate from 'climate only' to a systems view of multiple, interacting limits.
cards.counter: The specific boundary values carry real uncertainty, and some boundaries are global while others are really regional — the numbers are estimates, not constants.

cards.title: Half the nitrogen in you came from one factory process
cards.fact: The Haber-Bosch process (1909) pulls nitrogen from the air to make fertiliser — and now feeds roughly half the world.
cards.detail: Before it, crop yields were capped by natural nitrogen. Synthetic ammonia broke that ceiling; a large share of the nitrogen atoms in your body passed through this industrial reaction.
cards.deploy: One chemical process underpins modern food security — a striking dependency to put on the table.
cards.counter: It's double-edged: the same nitrogen runoff drives algal blooms, dead zones, and potent nitrous-oxide emissions.

cards.title: Reinforcing vs balancing feedback
cards.fact: Two loop types explain most system behaviour: one amplifies, one stabilises.
cards.detail: Reinforcing (positive) loops compound — interest, viral spread, arms races. Balancing (negative) loops push back toward a target — a thermostat, hunger, market correction.
cards.deploy: Lets you name why something grows explosively or stays stubbornly stable instead of hand-waving.
cards.counter: Real systems chain many loops with delays; reading off a single loop usually misleads.

cards.title: The tragedy of the commons — and its rebuttal
cards.fact: Shared resources get overused when each user pockets the gain but shares the cost — yet communities often solve this without the state or markets.
cards.detail: Hardin (1968) argued a shared pasture is doomed to overgrazing. Elinor Ostrom (Nobel 2009) then documented many real communities that govern shared fisheries, forests and irrigation sustainably through their own rules.
cards.deploy: Carries its own counter-argument: useful whether you're arguing for regulation OR for local self-governance.
cards.counter: Hardin overgeneralised from a model; Ostrom showed the 'tragedy' is not inevitable when users can communicate and make binding rules.

cards.title: Heavy tails: when the average lies
cards.fact: Wealth, city sizes, and word frequencies follow heavy-tailed distributions where a few cases dominate.
cards.detail: In a power-law-like distribution, the 'typical' value and the average can be wildly different — think the 80/20 rule. A handful of extreme cases carry most of the total.
cards.deploy: Warns against reasoning from the mean in unequal systems — 'average income' or 'average user' can be meaningless.
cards.counter: True power laws are statistically hard to distinguish from lognormal distributions, and the label is often slapped on data that doesn't fit it.

cards.title: Why the rich get richer
cards.fact: Why do a few get so much? Often because 'the rich get richer' — preferential attachment.
cards.detail: Power-law distributions frequently arise from one simple rule: the more you already have, the more you attract. New web pages link to already-popular pages; citations flow to already-cited papers; wealth begets wealth. Barabási and Albert (1999) showed this 'preferential attachment' generates the heavy-tailed, 'scale-free' patterns seen across many networks.
cards.deploy: A mechanism behind heavy tails: unequal outcomes can emerge from a neutral 'rich-get-richer' process, not just from differences in merit.
cards.counter: It's one route to power laws, not the only one; real systems mix it with chance, fitness and resets, so pure preferential attachment rarely fits perfectly.

quiz.q: Preferential attachment ('rich get richer') tends to produce…

cards.title: Where to push a system
cards.fact: There are places to push a system for big change — and the obvious ones are usually the weakest.
cards.detail: Donella Meadows ranked twelve 'leverage points' for intervening in a system. Tweaking numbers (taxes, subsidies) is low leverage; changing feedback loops and rules is stronger; the highest leverage is shifting the system's goals and the underlying paradigm. People sense these points but often push them the wrong way.
cards.deploy: A change toolkit: stop fiddling with parameters and aim at goals and mindsets, where leverage is greatest.
cards.counter: High-leverage points (paradigms) are exactly the hardest to move and easiest to get catastrophically wrong; the ranking is a heuristic, not a formula.

quiz.q: In Meadows' framework, the highest-leverage intervention is…
choices: Changing the system's goals or paradigm

cards.title: Governing the commons
cards.fact: Elinor Ostrom showed communities can govern shared resources themselves — and found the rules that make it work.
cards.detail: Against the idea that commons inevitably collapse, Ostrom's fieldwork on fisheries, forests and irrigation found communities sustainably self-governing for generations. Her eight design principles include clear boundaries, rules fitted to local conditions, participation in rule-making, monitoring, graduated sanctions, cheap conflict resolution and nested governance. She won the 2009 Nobel in economics.
cards.deploy: The empirical rebuttal to 'tragedy of the commons': self-organised governance is a real third option beyond the state and the market.
cards.counter: Her principles aren't a guarantee — they work best for bounded, local resources; scaling them to global commons like the climate is far harder.

quiz.q: Ostrom showed commons can be sustained by…
choices: Community self-governance with the right rules

cards.title: Climate tipping points
cards.fact: Push a natural system too far and it can flip — abruptly, and sometimes for good.
cards.detail: Some Earth systems have thresholds where change becomes self-reinforcing: melting ice exposes dark water that absorbs more heat; a drying Amazon can flip toward savanna; the Atlantic overturning circulation (AMOC) could slow sharply. Past a tipping point the shift can be fast and effectively irreversible, and crossing one can nudge others — a cascade.
cards.deploy: Why climate risk isn't smoothly proportional: some changes don't ease back once you stop pushing.
cards.counter: Exact thresholds are uncertain and hotly debated — some 'tipping' claims outrun the evidence, and timescales range from years to centuries.

quiz.q: A climate 'tipping point' is…
choices: A threshold past which change is self-reinforcing and often irreversible

cards.title: Keystone species
cards.fact: Some species hold a whole ecosystem together — far out of proportion to their numbers.
cards.detail: A 'keystone species' has an outsized effect relative to its abundance (Robert Paine, 1969). Remove sea otters and urchins strip the kelp forests; remove the ochre sea star and mussels crowd everyone out; remove wolves and herbivores reshape the land. Like the keystone of an arch, pull it and the structure can collapse.
cards.deploy: Explains why protecting one species can matter for a whole ecosystem — and why Yellowstone's wolves rippled so far.
cards.counter: The label is overused (200+ claimed keystones) and context-dependent; real food webs are messier than a single linchpin.

quiz.q: A keystone species is one that…
choices: Has an outsized effect relative to its abundance

cards.title: Fertiliser's dead zones
cards.fact: The fertiliser that feeds the world also chokes its waters — creating ocean 'dead zones'.
cards.detail: Nitrogen and phosphorus runoff from farms (and sewage) over-fertilise rivers, lakes and coasts. The nutrients trigger algal blooms; when the algae die and decompose they strip oxygen from the water, creating hypoxic 'dead zones' (like the Gulf of Mexico's) where fish can't survive. It's the downstream cost of Haber–Bosch abundance.
cards.deploy: The other half of the fertiliser story: the reactive nitrogen that feeds billions also pollutes the water that receives the runoff.
cards.counter: It's manageable, not inevitable — better nutrient timing, buffer strips and treatment cut runoff; the obstacle is mostly cost and governance, not chemistry.

quiz.q: Eutrophication creates 'dead zones' by…
choices: Nutrient runoff → algal blooms → oxygen depletion

cards.title: Comparative advantage
cards.fact: Two countries can both gain from trade even if one is better at making everything.
cards.detail: Ricardo (1817): what matters is opportunity cost, not absolute skill. Each side specialises where it gives up the least, and total output rises. It's the core case for trade.
cards.deploy: The standard answer to 'they can make it cheaper, so trade hurts us' — gains come from specialisation, not from winning at everything.
cards.counter: Named critics — Friedrich List in the 1840s, Ha-Joon Chang today — argue infant industries need protection to ever become competitive; and the clean result assumes full employment and mobile resources while ignoring distribution: trade can raise the total yet leave specific workers and regions worse off.

quiz.q: Comparative advantage says gains from trade come from differences in…
A country should specialise where it has the lowest…

cards.title: Externalities
cards.fact: When a cost or benefit lands on third parties, the market price gets it wrong.
cards.detail: Pollution is the classic case: a factory's price doesn't include the harm downstream. Pigou (1920) proposed taxing the activity to make the price tell the truth.
cards.deploy: Justifies carbon taxes, congestion charges, and the like: prices need correcting when costs spill over.
cards.counter: Coase (1960) showed that with clear property rights and low bargaining costs, private parties can fix externalities without taxes — the right remedy depends on the situation.

cards.title: Loss aversion
cards.fact: Losing $100 hurts about twice as much as gaining $100 feels good.
cards.detail: Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory (1979) showed people don't weigh outcomes by final wealth but by gains and losses from a reference point — and losses loom larger. It helped found behavioural economics.
cards.deploy: Undercuts the assumption that people are cool rational maximisers — framing a choice as a loss vs a gain changes behaviour.
cards.counter: The exact 2:1 ratio varies by context and there's ongoing replication debate; it's a robust tendency, not a fixed constant.

cards.title: Hume's is–ought gap
cards.fact: You can't logically derive what ought to be purely from what is.
cards.detail: Hume (1739) noticed writers slide from describing facts ('is') to prescribing duties ('ought') without justifying the jump. Facts alone don't entail values.
cards.deploy: A precision tool for spotting when an opponent smuggles a value claim in under cover of 'the science says'.
cards.counter: Some philosophers (ethical naturalists) argue the gap can be bridged; it's a powerful warning, not a settled proof that values float free of facts.

cards.title: Falsifiability
cards.fact: A claim that nothing could ever disprove isn't really scientific.
cards.detail: Popper argued the mark of a scientific theory is that it sticks its neck out — it forbids certain observations, so it could be proven wrong. 'What would change your mind?' is the key question.
cards.deploy: A sharp test against unfalsifiable claims ('it's true, you just can't see the evidence').
cards.counter: Kuhn and Lakatos showed real science doesn't work by naive falsification — a failed prediction is often blamed on auxiliary assumptions, not the core theory.

quiz.q: For Popper, a scientific theory must be…
By Popper's criterion, which claim is LEAST scientific (unfalsifiable)?
choices: Heavy objects fall at g in a vacuum
Whatever happens was meant to be
Water boils at 100°C at sea level

cards.title: Rawls's veil of ignorance
cards.fact: To find fair rules, choose them not knowing who you'll be in the society.
cards.detail: Rawls (1971): behind a 'veil' that hides your wealth, talents, race and class, you'd pick principles that protect everyone — because you might end up at the bottom.
cards.deploy: A portable fairness test for any institution or policy: would you accept it not knowing your place in it?
cards.counter: Nozick and others reject the setup: why assume people behind the veil would be so risk-averse (favouring the worst-off) rather than gambling on the average?

cards.title: The median voter theorem
cards.fact: In a simple two-way majority vote, the middle voter decides — so parties drift to the centre.
cards.detail: If opinion lines up on one axis and the winner needs a majority, the option preferred by the median voter beats all others. Candidates converge toward that voter to win.
cards.deploy: Explains why rival parties can end up sounding alike — a clean model for centrist convergence.
cards.counter: It assumes one dimension, two options, and full turnout. Primaries, multidimensional issues, and abstention routinely break it.

cards.title: Duverger's law
cards.fact: Winner-take-all elections tend to produce two big parties; proportional systems produce many.
cards.detail: Under first-past-the-post, votes for small parties are 'wasted', so voters and donors consolidate around two contenders. Proportional representation rewards smaller parties, so more survive.
cards.deploy: Shows that party systems are shaped by the voting rules, not just by the electorate's views — institutions matter.
cards.counter: It's a tendency, not an iron law: the UK and India sustain strong regional/third parties under the same rules.

cards.title: The collective action problem
cards.fact: Even when everyone would benefit, large groups often fail to act — because each person can free-ride.
cards.detail: Olson (1965): if you'll get the benefit whether or not you contribute, the rational move is to let others do the work. So big diffuse groups under-organise while small concentrated interests punch above their weight.
cards.deploy: Explains why concentrated lobbies beat diffuse majorities, and why obvious public goods get under-provided.
cards.counter: Selective incentives, social pressure, leadership, and repeated interaction (Ostrom) routinely overcome free-riding — it's a hurdle, not a wall.

cards.title: Arrow's impossibility theorem
cards.fact: No voting system can be perfectly fair — Arrow proved it's mathematically impossible.
cards.detail: Arrow's impossibility theorem (1951): with three or more options, no ranked voting method can satisfy a short list of reasonable conditions at once — no dictator, respect unanimity, and 'independence of irrelevant alternatives'. Every ranked system trades something off (and has a spoiler effect). It's a foundational result in social choice.
cards.deploy: Ends the hunt for a 'perfect' voting system — the real question is which trade-offs you accept, not whether you can avoid them.
cards.counter: It applies to ranked orderings; rated systems (approval, score voting) that use grades rather than rankings sidestep the exact theorem, so it's not a counsel of despair.

quiz.q: Arrow's impossibility theorem shows that…
choices: No ranked voting rule can meet all fairness criteria at once

cards.title: Proportional representation's trade-off
cards.fact: Proportional representation trades the stability of two big parties for fuller representation.
cards.detail: Where winner-take-all tends toward two parties (Duverger), proportional representation allocates seats in line with vote share, so smaller parties win seats and parliaments hold many. That mirrors diverse views more faithfully and wastes fewer votes, but usually means coalition governments — more inclusive, sometimes less decisive. It's the central trade-off in electoral-system design.
cards.deploy: Frames the electoral-system choice: representativeness (PR) versus governability and clear accountability (FPTP) — no free lunch.
cards.counter: It's a tendency, not a law: PR systems vary hugely (thresholds, district size) and many are perfectly stable; 'PR equals chaos' is a caricature.

quiz.q: Compared with winner-take-all, proportional representation tends to produce…

cards.title: You never test one idea alone
cards.fact: A failed experiment never cleanly refutes a single hypothesis — you always test a whole bundle.
cards.detail: The Duhem–Quine thesis: any prediction leans on a web of auxiliary assumptions (the instrument works, no other forces, the background theory holds). When a test fails, logic alone can't say which link broke — you can always save the core idea by blaming an auxiliary. This complicates Popper's clean falsification and feeds Kuhn's picture of theories defended within a 'paradigm' until anomalies pile up.
cards.deploy: A check on naive falsification: 'the experiment disproved it' is rarely as clean as it sounds.
cards.counter: It can be overstated into 'anything goes' — in practice scientists do reach justified verdicts; the holism is real but not paralysing.

quiz.q: The Duhem–Quine thesis says a failed test…
choices: Can't pinpoint which assumption failed — you test a whole web

cards.title: The naturalistic fallacy
cards.fact: Calling something 'natural' doesn't make it good — and defining 'good' as any natural property is a trap.
cards.detail: G.E. Moore's naturalistic fallacy (1903): you can't define 'good' as identical to a natural property (pleasure, survival, what evolution favours), because his 'open question' always remains — 'this is pleasant, but is it good?' still makes sense, so the two aren't the same. It's cousin to Hume's is–ought gap and to the everyday 'appeal to nature' (natural = better).
cards.deploy: Disarms 'it's natural, therefore good/right' arguments — and warns against reading ethics straight off biology.
cards.counter: Ethical naturalists reject Moore's argument and hold that moral facts can be natural facts; the 'fallacy' label is itself contested (Frankena).

quiz.q: The 'naturalistic fallacy' warns against…
choices: Equating 'good' with a natural property (e.g. 'natural = good')

cards.title: Nozick's reply to Rawls
cards.fact: Nozick's reply to Rawls: a just outcome is whatever free exchanges produce — even if unequal.
cards.detail: In Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), Robert Nozick countered Rawls with an 'entitlement theory': holdings are just if they were acquired and transferred justly, whatever pattern results. His 'Wilt Chamberlain' example: if fans freely pay to watch a star, the resulting inequality is just, and forcibly redistributing it violates liberty. He defends only a 'minimal state'.
cards.deploy: The libertarian counterweight to Rawls: justice as fair process and liberty, not as a fair distribution pattern.
cards.counter: Egalitarians like G.A. Cohen argue that 'just steps' ignore tainted starting points (conquest, slavery) and that pure process can entrench injustice; Nozick's initial-acquisition principle is the weak link.

quiz.q: Nozick's entitlement theory judges a distribution by…
choices: Whether it arose through just acquisition and free transfer

cards.title: What economics is about
cards.fact: Economics starts from one awkward fact: we have unlimited wants and limited means.
cards.detail: Because you can't have everything, every choice means giving something up. Economics studies how people and societies handle those trade-offs — and the cost of any choice is the best alternative you gave up (its opportunity cost).
cards.deploy: Reframes almost any policy fight as 'what are we giving up?' rather than just 'is this nice?'.
cards.counter: The scarcity frame can hide questions of power and distribution — who decides what's scarce, and for whom.

quiz.q: The opportunity cost of a choice is…
choices: The best alternative you gave up

quiz.q: Economics begins from the problem of…

cards.title: Supply and demand
cards.fact: In the basic model, price isn't set by cost or fairness — it's where supply meets demand.
cards.detail: When price rises, buyers want less and sellers offer more; the price settles where the two meet. It's a powerful starting model — but it assumes competition, good information and flexible prices that real markets often lack.
cards.deploy: Explains how a price emerges from supply and demand — and why interventions like caps or subsidies ripple into quantity (shortages or surpluses), not just price.
cards.counter: Perfect competition is rare; with market power, information gaps or sticky prices the simple model can mislead.

quiz.q: In the basic model, the market price settles where…

cards.title: What GDP measures
cards.fact: GDP measures the money value of what a country produces — and quietly leaves a lot out.
cards.detail: GDP totals the market value of a country's output. It misses unpaid work, ignores distribution, and treats some harms as gains — which is why 'growth' is one of economics' biggest arguments.
cards.deploy: Cuts through 'the economy grew, so we're better off' — ask what the number counts and what it omits.
cards.counter: For all its flaws, GDP tracks real things — jobs, output, tax revenue — and no rival measure has cleanly replaced it.

quiz.q: GDP does NOT directly count…

cards.title: Why 'political economy'?
cards.fact: Before it was 'economics', it was 'political economy' — and the politics never really left.
cards.detail: The classical writers studied 'political economy' — wealth and its distribution between classes. Around 1900 the field rebranded as 'economics' on the model of physics, pushing power to the margins; 'political economy' names the traditions that keep it central.
cards.deploy: Reminds an opponent that 'just the economics' is rarely just the economics.
cards.counter: Naming the politics doesn't settle the facts — efficiency and distribution can still be studied with evidence.

cards.title: The rival schools
cards.fact: There is no single 'economics' — there are rival schools that disagree about how the economy works.
cards.detail: Economics is plural: classical, Marxian, neoclassical, Keynesian, monetarist, Austrian, behavioural and ecological schools give different answers to the same questions. The mainstream is one paradigm among several, not the last word.
cards.deploy: Whenever someone says 'economists agree', ask which economists — the field is plural.
cards.counter: Pluralism can tip into 'anything goes'; some claims really are better supported by the evidence than others.

cards.title: Adam Smith and the invisible hand
cards.fact: Smith argued a butcher feeds you not from kindness but from self-interest — and somehow it works.
cards.detail: Smith (1776) argued self-interested exchange, coordinated 'as if by an invisible hand', can benefit all, powered by the division of labour. But he also rooted society in sympathy and distrusted merchants — he's far more nuanced than the caricature.
cards.deploy: Useful against caricatures of 'capitalism = greed is good' — even Smith didn't say that.
cards.counter: Smith still defended self-interest and markets as broadly benign — he isn't the proto-socialist some make him either.

quiz.q: Smith's 'invisible hand' is the idea that…

cards.title: The division of labour
cards.fact: Smith watched a pin factory and saw the secret of modern wealth: split the job up.
cards.detail: Splitting work into specialised steps multiplies output — Smith's pin factory is the classic example. But he and later Marx warned it can also deskill and alienate the worker.
cards.deploy: Explains assembly lines, supply chains and outsourcing — and their human downside.
cards.counter: Specialisation also lifted billions out of subsistence; the gains are real, not just the costs.

cards.title: Ricardo and the logic machine
cards.fact: David Ricardo turned economics into a machine of pure logic — and reached unsettling conclusions.
cards.detail: Ricardo built ruthless logical models: comparative advantage, the theory of rent (landlords gain as population grows), and a labour theory of value later taken up by Marx and dropped by the mainstream.
cards.deploy: Shows distribution-as-class-conflict has deep roots inside classical economics, not just in Marx.
cards.counter: The labour theory of value faces hard problems (capital, time, skill) that marginalism was designed to solve.

cards.title: Where does value come from?
cards.fact: Is a thing valuable because of the work in it, or because of how much you want it?
cards.detail: Classical economists and Marx located value in labour; marginalists from the 1870s relocated it in usefulness at the margin. The mainstream took the second path — but the first still frames profit as extraction rather than reward.
cards.deploy: Lets you locate an argument: profit-as-reward (marginalist) vs profit-as-extraction (Marxian).
cards.counter: Marginalism resolved real puzzles — like why water is cheap and diamonds dear — that the labour theory struggled with.

cards.title: The marginal revolution (1870s)
cards.fact: In the 1870s economics quietly changed its mind about what value even is.
cards.detail: Around 1871–1874, Jevons, Menger and Walras relocated value in marginal utility, founding neoclassical economics and shifting the field from class and distribution toward individual optimisation and equilibrium.
cards.deploy: Explains why mainstream economics talks about utility and equilibrium rather than class.
cards.counter: The marginalist tools genuinely unified price theory and remain the workhorse of applied economics.

cards.title: Marx's Capital
cards.fact: Marx didn't just dislike capitalism — he tried to reverse-engineer its hidden machinery.
cards.detail: Marx (1867) argued workers produce more value than their wage ('surplus value'), the source of profit and capital; competition drives accumulation, crises and concentration. His critique outlived his failed predictions.
cards.deploy: A structured frame for arguments about exploitation, inequality and recurring financial crises.
cards.counter: Where Marxist regimes took power, central planning produced its own shortages and repression — the cure has a grim record too.

quiz.q: For Marx, profit ('surplus value') comes from…
choices: Value workers produce above their wage

cards.title: Historical materialism
cards.fact: Marx's big bet: to understand history, follow how people make their living.
cards.detail: Historical materialism holds that the economic base shapes a society's politics and ideas, and that history advances as productive forces outgrow old ownership arrangements. Powerful as a habit of analysis, contested as a law of history.
cards.deploy: Prompts the sharp question: 'whose material interests does this idea serve?'.
cards.counter: Culture, religion and ideas have driven huge changes no economic base predicted.

cards.title: Keynes and the stuck economy
cards.fact: Keynes argued a market economy can get stuck in a slump — and just sit there.
cards.detail: Keynes (1936) argued economies can settle below full employment when demand collapses, so government should boost demand in slumps. Dominant until 1970s stagflation, revived after 2008.
cards.deploy: The canonical case for stimulus in a recession — private demand can fail to recover by itself.
cards.counter: Sustained deficit spending can stoke inflation and debt; the 1970s showed demand management has limits.

quiz.q: Keynes argued that in a slump, the economy…
choices: Can stay stuck below full employment

quiz.q: Keynes's prescription for a demand-deficient slump was…
choices: Cut public spending to balance the budget
Government spending to lift aggregate demand
Wait for wages to fall on their own

cards.title: The paradox of thrift
cards.fact: If everyone saves more at once, the country can end up saving less.
cards.detail: Saving is prudent for one household but, if everyone does it at once in a slump, spending and incomes fall and total saving can drop — a 'fallacy of composition' Keynes used to justify stimulus.
cards.deploy: Explains why 'everyone should just budget like a household' fails for a whole economy at once.
cards.counter: In normal times saving does finance investment; the paradox is a slump phenomenon, not a general law.

cards.title: Friedman and monetarism
cards.fact: Milton Friedman's counter-revolution: inflation is always, everywhere, about money.
cards.detail: Friedman argued inflation is fundamentally monetary and government meddling does more harm than good. Strict monetarism failed in practice, but his free-market politics shaped the neoliberal era.
cards.deploy: The standard hawkish case that loose money, not greedy sellers, drives inflation.
cards.counter: Keynesian economists like James Tobin disputed the tight money–inflation link; in practice supply shocks and expectations matter, and central banks abandoned strict monetary targets when they failed to hold.

cards.title: Hayek and the knowledge problem
cards.fact: Hayek's argument against central planning: nobody knows enough — but prices do.
cards.detail: Hayek (1945) argued that dispersed knowledge makes central planning impossible, while prices coordinate it automatically — a deep case for markets that information economists like Joseph Stiglitz later qualified, citing externalities, monopoly and imperfect information.
cards.deploy: The strongest principled argument against detailed central planning — it's a knowledge problem, not just a motivation one.
cards.counter: Information economists like Joseph Stiglitz showed markets with imperfect information aren't efficient either; and prices routinely misprice externalities and public goods — which is why even market economies regulate.

cards.title: The hockey stick
cards.fact: For most of history, ordinary living standards barely moved. Then, around 1800, they exploded.
cards.detail: After millennia of near-flat living standards, sustained growth began with Britain's Industrial Revolution (~1800), lifting output per person many-fold — at an immense early human and environmental cost.
cards.deploy: Anchors any argument about technology and growth — the modern world is a recent, fragile exception.
cards.counter: The early human costs were immense, and the gains spread very unevenly across people and regions.

quiz.q: The 'hockey stick' of economic history refers to…
choices: Living standards flat for millennia then rising sharply

cards.title: Enclosure and the making of workers
cards.fact: Before there were factory workers, common land had to be fenced off — and people pushed into wage labour.
cards.detail: English enclosure (1500s–1800s) privatised common land, creating a wage-dependent workforce — Marx's 'primitive accumulation'. Read either as an efficiency gain or as mass dispossession.
cards.deploy: Reminds us markets in land and labour were created — often by force — not simply 'natural'.
cards.counter: Enclosure also raised food output sharply at a time of rising population; it wasn't pure loss.

cards.title: Bretton Woods and the end of gold
cards.fact: For 27 years the world's money was anchored to gold through the dollar — until one night in 1971 it wasn't.
cards.detail: Bretton Woods (1944) pegged currencies to a gold-backed dollar; Nixon ended gold convertibility in 1971 and money became pure fiat. Whether money needs a hard anchor is still argued.
cards.deploy: Background for any argument about fiat money, inflation, gold standards or cryptocurrencies.
cards.counter: Gold standards impose harsh discipline that can deepen depressions; 'sound money' has real costs too.

cards.title: The Great Depression
cards.fact: The 1930s slump was so deep it rewrote economics — and economists still argue about why.
cards.detail: The 1930s Depression — mass unemployment after the 1929 crash — birthed Keynesianism and the activist state. Its causes (demand collapse, monetary contraction, the gold standard) remain contested.
cards.deploy: Every modern crisis response (2008, 2020) is haunted by 'don't repeat the 1930s'.
cards.counter: There's no settled single cause — demand, money, banking and the gold standard all played a part.

cards.title: The 1970s stagflation
cards.fact: In the 1970s, prices and unemployment rose together — which the textbooks said couldn't happen.
cards.detail: 1970s stagflation — high inflation and unemployment together — broke the simple Phillips curve, discredited naive Keynesianism, and ushered in monetarism and the free-market turn.
cards.deploy: The go-to counter to naive Keynesianism — and the origin story of modern central banking.
cards.counter: Stagflation was driven heavily by oil shocks; it didn't prove demand management is always wrong.

cards.title: The neoliberal turn
cards.fact: Around 1980, the rich world swung from 'manage the market' to 'free the market'.
cards.detail: From ~1980, Thatcher and Reagan drove privatisation, tax cuts, deregulation and weaker unions, drawing on Friedman and Hayek. Credited with taming inflation, blamed for inequality and the 2008 crisis.
cards.deploy: Names the framework most current economic arguments are still reacting for or against.
cards.counter: It's a loose, contested label: its architects (Friedman, Hayek, Thatcher, Reagan) sold it as freeing growth, while critics like Joseph Stiglitz and Naomi Klein blame it for inequality and financial crises — and results varied enormously by country.

cards.title: The 2008 financial crisis
cards.fact: In 2008 the financial system nearly stopped — and the faith that markets police themselves took a beating.
cards.detail: A 2008 mortgage bubble froze global finance and triggered the worst slump since the 1930s. The bailout-and-stimulus response revived Keynes and dented 'efficient markets' faith; its causes and the later austerity remain contested.
cards.deploy: The modern reference point for financial regulation, bailouts and 'too big to fail'.
cards.counter: Causes are contested — reckless private finance, or government distortions and easy money, or both.

cards.title: A letter is a number you don't know yet
cards.fact: A variable like x is just a placeholder standing in for a number.
cards.detail: A variable is a name for a number. Writing \(2x\) means 'two times x', whatever x turns out to be. An expression like \(3x + 5\) is a recipe: feed in a number for \(x\) and it gives one out — if \(x = 4\), then \(3x + 5 = 17\). The point of a letter is generality: \(A = \pi r^2\) gives the area of every circle in one line, instead of a separate sum for each radius.

media.caption: An expression is a recipe; plug in a value.

cards.deploy: Lets one statement cover every case at once — the move from arithmetic to algebra.
cards.counter: A symbol only helps if you track what it stands for and its units; the same letter meaning two different things inside one argument is a classic error.

quiz.q: If x = 4, what is 3x + 5?

cards.title: An equation is a balance scale
cards.fact: Whatever you do to one side of an equation, do to the other — and it stays true.
cards.detail: An equation says two things are equal. \(x + 3 = 7\) reads 'some number plus 3 equals 7'. Think of \(=\) as the pivot of a balance: the two sides weigh the same. To find \(x\), undo what surrounds it by doing the same thing to both sides. Subtract 3 from each: \(x + 3 - 3 = 7 - 3\), so \(x = 4\). The scale never tips because you changed both sides equally. That single habit — do the same to both sides — solves most of school algebra.

media.caption: Subtract 3 from both sides to isolate x.

cards.deploy: Turns 'solving for x' into a mechanical routine: isolate the unknown by undoing operations symmetrically.
cards.counter: Balance holds only for reversible operations applied equally. Multiplying both sides by zero, or by an unknown that might be zero, can erase real solutions or invent fake ones.

quiz.q: To solve x + 3 = 7, you…

cards.title: A function is a machine
cards.fact: Put a number in, get exactly one number out — that's a function.
cards.detail: Write \(f(x)\) — read 'f of x' — for the output when the input is \(x\). The rule \(f(x) = 2x + 1\) doubles the input and adds one, so \(f(3) = 7\). 'Exactly one output' is the whole idea: a function never returns two answers for the same input. Lay the input along the bottom and the output up the side and you get a graph — a picture of the rule. Functions are the things calculus and machine learning act on.

media.caption: f(x) = 2x + 1 — one output for every input.

cards.deploy: Names the basic object of all higher maths: a dependable input→output rule you can graph, combine and analyse.
cards.counter: A relation that gives two outputs for one input (like 'a number's square roots', ±) is not a function — distinguishing the two avoids real mistakes.

quiz.q: For f(x) = 2x + 1, what is f(3)?

cards.title: Powers and roots
cards.fact: A power is repeated multiplication; a root undoes it.
cards.detail: \(a^n\) means multiply \(a\) by itself \(n\) times: \(2^3 = 2\times2\times2 = 8\), and \(2^{10} = 1024\). The square root undoes squaring: \(\sqrt{9} = 3\) because \(3^2 = 9\). Powers of the same base add when you multiply: \(a^m \cdot a^n = a^{m+n}\). This is what lets us write the huge and the tiny compactly — scientific notation: \(6.02\times10^{23}\) particles, or \(10^{-9}\) for a billionth.

media.say: a-to-the-m times a-to-the-n equals a-to-the-(m plus n).
media.caption: Multiplying powers adds the exponents.
2ˣ explodes — each step doubles the last.

cards.deploy: Compresses repeated multiplication and gives a clean way to handle very large or very small numbers.
cards.counter: Sign and fraction rules trip people up: \(a^0 = 1\), a negative exponent means a reciprocal (\(a^{-1} = 1/a\)), and a fractional one means a root (\(a^{1/2} = \sqrt a\)).

quiz.q: What is 2¹⁰?

cards.title: Logarithms: the inverse of powers
cards.fact: A logarithm answers one question: what power produces this number?
cards.detail: \(\log_{10} 1000 = 3\) because \(10^3 = 1000\). The log is the exponent. Its key trick is turning multiplication into addition: \(\log(ab) = \log a + \log b\). A log scale (decibels, the Richter scale, pH) spaces powers of ten evenly, so 10 and 1000 sit the same distance apart, which tames quantities that span many orders of magnitude. In machine learning logs are everywhere — they turn long products of probabilities into manageable sums.

media.say: log-base-b of x-times-y equals log of x plus log of y.
media.caption: Logs convert products into sums.
The logarithm: quick to rise, then a slow crawl.

cards.deploy: Lets you read quantities that span orders of magnitude, and replace awkward products with sums.
cards.counter: Logs are only defined for positive numbers, and the base matters: base 10, base 2 and the natural base \(e\) differ by a constant factor, so always say which you mean.

quiz.q: What is log₁₀(1000)?

cards.title: The straight line: y = mx + b
cards.fact: Every straight line is y = mx + b: m is the slope, b is where it crosses the axis.
cards.detail: The slope \(m\) is rise over run — how much \(y\) climbs for each step right. The intercept \(b\) is the value of \(y\) when \(x = 0\), where the line meets the vertical axis. So \(y = 2x + 1\) starts at 1 and climbs 2 for every 1 across. A bigger \(m\) tilts the line steeper; a negative \(m\) sends it downhill. This is the simplest model in all of statistics and machine learning — a prediction that changes at a constant rate.

media.caption: Drag m and b: the line tilts and shifts.

cards.deploy: The default first model whenever one quantity changes steadily with another.
cards.counter: Most real relationships aren't straight; a line is a deliberately simple approximation, useful precisely because it has just two numbers to find.

quiz.q: In y = mx + b, what does b represent?
choices: Where the line crosses the y-axis

cards.title: Curves and the quadratic
cards.fact: Add an x² term and the straight line bends into a parabola.
cards.detail: \(y = ax^2 + bx + c\) traces a parabola — a U-shaped curve. The coefficient \(a\) sets how narrow it is and which way it opens (up if \(a>0\), down if \(a<0\)); \(c\) shifts it vertically. To find where it crosses zero, the quadratic formula gives the answer for any quadratic: \(x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}\). Parabolas describe thrown objects, and the U-shape is exactly the kind of curve machine learning slides down to find its best fit.

media.caption: y = ax² + bx + c — change a, b, c to reshape the parabola.

cards.deploy: The first step beyond straight lines, and the shape of the cost surfaces optimisers descend.
cards.counter: The quadratic formula's discriminant \(b^2 - 4ac\) can be negative — then the curve never crosses zero and the (real) solutions don't exist.

quiz.q: The graph of y = ax² + bx + c is a…

cards.title: Sigma notation: add up a list
cards.fact: The symbol Σ is shorthand for 'add up all of these'.
cards.detail: \(\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i\) means add \(x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n\). The \(i\) is a counter that runs from the bottom number to the top one. For example \(\sum_{i=1}^{4} i = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10\). The average of \(n\) numbers is just \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_i x_i\). This one symbol runs through all of statistics and machine learning: every total error, mean, and dot product is a sum written this way.

media.say: the sum of x-one, x-two, and so on up to x-n.
media.caption: Sigma says: run the counter and add.
Σ adds the bars: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10.

cards.deploy: Compresses 'add up many terms' into one symbol you'll meet in every quantitative field.
cards.counter: The limits and the index matter: \(\sum_{i=0}\) versus \(\sum_{i=1}\), or summing the wrong variable, silently changes the result.

quiz.q: What does Σ (from i=1 to 4) of i equal?

cards.title: The limit: getting infinitely close
cards.fact: A limit is the value a function heads toward as the input creeps up to a point.
cards.detail: Sometimes a function misbehaves exactly at one point but behaves perfectly all around it. \(\frac{\sin x}{x}\) reads as \(0/0\) at \(x = 0\), yet as \(x\) shrinks toward zero the ratio heads steadily to 1. The limit, written \(\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{\sin x}{x} = 1\), captures that destination without ever dividing by zero. Making 'infinitely close' precise is the foundation the rest of calculus stands on.

media.caption: Undefined at 0, yet it heads to 1.
sin(x)/x has a hole at 0, yet heads to 1.

cards.deploy: Lets you reason about behaviour at a point a function can't actually reach — the gateway to derivatives and integrals.
cards.counter: A limit can fail to exist: if a function jumps, or approaches different values from the left and the right, there is no single destination.

quiz.q: A limit describes the value a function…
choices: Heads toward as the input approaches a point

cards.title: The derivative: the slope of a curve
cards.fact: The derivative is how fast something is changing right now — the slope of a curve at a point.
cards.detail: A straight line has one slope everywhere. A curve's steepness keeps changing. The derivative \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) (also written \(f'(x)\)) is the slope of the tangent line that just grazes the curve at a single point. You find it by taking the slope between two nearby points and letting them slide together — a limit. For \(f(x) = x^2\), the derivative is \(f'(x) = 2x\): at \(x = 3\) the curve climbs with slope 6. Speed is the derivative of distance; acceleration is the derivative of speed.

media.say: f-prime of x equals the limit, as h shrinks to zero, of the change in f divided by h.
media.caption: The slope between two points, as they merge.
Slide the point — the tangent's slope is the derivative.

cards.deploy: The universal tool for rates of change: speed, growth, marginal cost, and the direction to adjust a model.
cards.counter: A derivative needs a smooth curve. At a sharp corner or a jump the slope isn't defined — the function is not differentiable there.

quiz.q: The derivative of a function at a point is the…

cards.title: The integral: area under a curve
cards.fact: The integral adds up infinitely many thin slivers to measure the area under a curve.
cards.detail: To find the area under a graph, slice the region into thin rectangles, add their areas, then let the slices grow infinitely thin so the answer becomes exact. That limit is the integral, \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\). The fundamental theorem of calculus ties it to the derivative: integration and differentiation undo each other. Distance is the integral of speed over time; in probability, the chance of landing in a range is the area under a curve.

media.caption: The shaded area is the integral ∫ f(x) dx.

cards.deploy: Turns a rate into a total: accumulate speed into distance, a density into a probability, a flow into a quantity.
cards.counter: Many functions have no tidy antiderivative formula — real integrals are often computed numerically rather than solved on paper.

quiz.q: An integral computes the…

cards.title: The chain rule: rates that pass through layers
cards.fact: To differentiate a function inside a function, multiply the two rates of change.
cards.detail: If \(y\) depends on \(u\), and \(u\) depends on \(x\), then a small nudge in \(x\) ripples through both: \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du}\cdot\frac{du}{dx}\). Take \(y = (3x+1)^2\): the outer squaring contributes \(2(3x+1)\), the inner \(3x+1\) contributes \(3\), and the product is \(6(3x+1)\). The chain rule is how rates compose through nested steps — and it is exactly the mechanism that trains deep neural networks, where the error is passed back layer by layer (backpropagation).

media.say: the rate of f-of-g equals f's rate (at g) times g's rate.
media.caption: Outer rate times inner rate.
A chain x → u → y; the rates multiply along it.

cards.deploy: Differentiates any composition — and underpins backpropagation, the engine of modern AI training.
cards.counter: It's easy to forget the inner derivative \(g'(x)\); leaving it out is one of the most common calculus mistakes.

quiz.q: The chain rule differentiates f(g(x)) as…

cards.title: The gradient: which way is uphill
cards.fact: The gradient bundles a function's slopes in every direction into one arrow pointing straight uphill.
cards.detail: When a function has several inputs, say \(f(x, y)\), it has a separate slope in the x-direction and in the y-direction — its partial derivatives. The gradient \(\nabla f\) collects them into a vector: \(\nabla f = \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right)\). That vector points in the direction of steepest increase, and its length tells you how steep. Walk in the opposite direction and you go downhill fastest — the single idea behind training almost every machine-learning model.

media.say: grad-f is the pair of slopes: how f changes along x, and along y.
media.caption: A vector of partial slopes, pointing uphill.
On the bowl f = x² + y², ∇f points outward — straight uphill.

cards.deploy: Gives the direction to step when tuning many numbers at once — the basis of gradient descent.
cards.counter: The gradient only shows the best local direction; on a bumpy surface, following it can stall in a dip that isn't the lowest point overall.

quiz.q: The gradient of a function points in the direction of…

cards.title: A vector is an arrow and a list
cards.fact: A vector is at once an arrow with direction and length, and a list of numbers.
cards.detail: In the plane, a vector points from the origin to a spot: \(\vec v = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}\) means 'go 3 right and 2 up'. The arrow picture (direction and length) and the column of numbers are the same object — and holding both views at once is what makes linear algebra work. A data point with many features (age, height, income…) is simply a vector with many entries: a single point in a high-dimensional space.

media.caption: The vector [3, 2] as an arrow from the origin.

cards.deploy: The basic unit of data and geometry alike: one object you can picture as an arrow or compute with as numbers.
cards.counter: The arrow picture is honest only up to three dimensions; beyond that you must trust the numbers, since a 300-feature vector has no drawable shape.

quiz.q: The vector [3, 2] describes…

cards.title: Adding and scaling vectors
cards.fact: Add vectors tip-to-tail; scale one by stretching or flipping it.
cards.detail: To add \(\vec a + \vec b\), set \(\vec b\)'s tail at \(\vec a\)'s tip; the sum runs from the very start to the very end. In numbers you just add matching entries: \(\begin{bmatrix}3\\1\end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}4\\3\end{bmatrix}\). Multiplying by a plain number (a scalar) stretches or flips: \(2\vec a\) is twice as long, \(-\vec a\) points the other way. Any weighted mix \(c_1\vec a + c_2\vec b\) — a 'linear combination' — is the core move of the whole subject.

media.caption: a + b, tip-to-tail.

cards.deploy: The two operations every later idea is built from: combine vectors and rescale them.
cards.counter: You can only add vectors of the same length (same number of entries); a 2-D and a 3-D vector have no defined sum.

cards.title: The dot product: how aligned are two vectors
cards.fact: The dot product is one number saying how much two vectors point the same way.
cards.detail: Multiply matching entries and add them up: \(\vec a \cdot \vec b = \sum_i a_i b_i\). The same number also equals \(|\vec a|\,|\vec b|\cos\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between the vectors. So the dot product is large when they align, zero when they're perpendicular (\(\cos 90^\circ = 0\)), and negative when they oppose. It is the standard measure of similarity: search engines and language models compare meanings by taking dot products of vectors.

media.tex: \vec a \cdot \vec b = \sum_i a_i b_i = |\vec a|\,|\vec b|\cos\theta
media.say: a dot b: multiply matching entries and add — also the lengths times the cosine of the angle between them.
media.caption: Two views: entry-by-entry, and angle-based.
Swing θ: the dot product peaks when aligned, hits 0 at 90°.

cards.deploy: The workhorse of similarity and projection — and the operation inside every matrix multiply and attention score.
cards.counter: A dot product near zero means the vectors are merely perpendicular, not that either is small; alignment and magnitude are different things.

quiz.q: The dot product of two perpendicular vectors is…

cards.title: Length and distance
cards.fact: A vector's norm is its length — and the gap between two points is the norm of their difference.
cards.detail: The norm \(\|\vec v\| = \sqrt{v_1^2 + v_2^2 + \cdots}\) is the Pythagorean theorem in any number of dimensions. The distance between two points is the norm of their difference, \(\|\vec a - \vec b\|\). 'Nearest neighbour' methods, clustering, and the size of an error all rest on this. Neatly, \(\|\vec v\|^2 = \vec v \cdot \vec v\): a vector's squared length is its dot product with itself.

media.say: the length of v is the square root of the sum of its squared entries.
media.caption: Pythagoras, in any number of dimensions.
‖[4, 3]‖ = √(16 + 9) = 5 — the hypotenuse.

cards.deploy: Defines size and closeness for data — the basis of distance, error magnitude and similarity searches.
cards.counter: The straight-line (Euclidean) norm is only one choice; others, like summing absolute values (the 'taxicab' norm), measure distance differently and suit different problems.

quiz.q: The norm of a vector measures its…

cards.title: A matrix is a grid of numbers
cards.fact: A matrix is a rectangular grid of numbers — a table, or a row of vectors side by side.
cards.detail: A matrix has rows and columns: \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\) is 2 by 2. You can read it as a spreadsheet — each row a record, each column a feature — or as several column vectors standing together. Its real power, though, is as an action: a matrix is a rule that takes a vector in and gives a transformed vector out, which is the next step.

media.caption: A 2×2 matrix: rows and columns.

cards.deploy: The container for data tables and for transformations alike — the central object of linear algebra.
cards.counter: Shape is everything: a 2×3 and a 3×2 matrix hold the same six numbers but behave completely differently, and most operations demand matching shapes.

quiz.q: A matrix is best described as…
choices: A grid of numbers in rows and columns

cards.title: A matrix transforms space
cards.fact: Multiplying a matrix by a vector moves the whole grid — it rotates, stretches and shears space.
cards.detail: \(A\vec x\) builds a new vector by combining \(A\)'s columns, each weighted by an entry of \(\vec x\). Picture it geometrically: the matrix moves every point of the plane at once, so the square grid tilts and stretches — yet straight lines stay straight and the origin stays fixed. That is a 'linear transformation'. The columns of \(A\) are nothing more than where the two basis arrows land after the move.

media.caption: Move the matrix [[a, b], [c, d]] — watch the grid transform.

cards.deploy: Reframes a matrix as a verb, not a table: it does something to space. This view unlocks the rest of the subject.
cards.counter: Only transformations that keep grid lines straight and evenly spaced, fixing the origin, are 'linear' — bends, curves and shifts of the origin are not matrix multiplication.

quiz.q: Multiplying a vector by a matrix geometrically…

cards.title: Matrix multiplication = doing one transform after another
cards.fact: Multiplying matrices means applying one transformation, then the next.
cards.detail: The product \(AB\) is the single transformation 'do \(B\) first, then \(A\)': \((AB)\vec x = A(B\vec x)\). Each entry of the product is a dot product of a row of \(A\) with a column of \(B\). Order matters — \(AB \neq BA\) in general, just as rotating then stretching differs from stretching then rotating. Chaining matrices this way is exactly how a neural network stacks its layers.

media.caption: The product is composition: B first, then A.

cards.deploy: Lets you collapse a whole pipeline of transformations into one matrix — and explains layered models.
cards.counter: Matrix multiplication is not commutative: swapping the order usually changes the result, and often isn't even allowed if the shapes stop matching.

quiz.q: In general, for matrices, AB is…

cards.title: Identity and inverse: undoing a transformation
cards.fact: The identity matrix changes nothing; the inverse runs a transformation backwards.
cards.detail: The identity matrix \(I\) has 1s down the diagonal and 0s elsewhere, so \(I\vec x = \vec x\) — the linear-algebra version of multiplying by 1. The inverse \(A^{-1}\) reverses whatever \(A\) did: \(A A^{-1} = I\). Not every matrix has one. If a transformation squashes space flat — collapsing a dimension — there is no way back, and no inverse exists. That collapse is detected by the determinant being zero.

media.say: A times A-inverse gives the identity — the do-nothing matrix.
media.caption: The inverse cancels the transformation.

cards.deploy: The formal 'undo' button — and the route to solving equations and reversing models.
cards.counter: Inverting a matrix that is nearly singular (almost flattening) is numerically unstable; in practice solvers avoid forming \(A^{-1}\) directly.

quiz.q: A matrix times its inverse gives the…

cards.title: Solving many equations at once: Ax = b
cards.fact: A pile of linear equations packs into one tidy matrix equation, Ax = b.
cards.detail: Two equations like \(2x + y = 5\) and \(x - y = 1\) fold into \(A\vec x = \vec b\), with \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(\vec b = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\). Solving asks: which input \(\vec x\) does \(A\) send to \(\vec b\)? If \(A\) is invertible, \(\vec x = A^{-1}\vec b\); otherwise there may be no solution, or infinitely many. Fitting a model, balancing a chemical equation and rendering 3-D graphics all reduce to solving \(A\vec x = \vec b\).

media.tex: A\vec x = \vec b \;\Rightarrow\; \vec x = A^{-1}\vec b
media.say: A times x equals b, so x equals A-inverse times b.
media.caption: When A is invertible, the system has one solution.
Two equations, two lines — they cross at the solution (2, 1).

cards.deploy: The standard form that an enormous range of practical problems gets rewritten into and solved.
cards.counter: Real systems are often 'overdetermined' — more equations than unknowns, no exact solution — so we settle for the closest fit instead (least squares).

quiz.q: In Ax = b, if A is invertible the solution is…

cards.title: The determinant: how much area gets scaled
cards.fact: The determinant says how much a transformation scales area — and zero means it flattens space.
cards.detail: For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}\), the determinant is \(\det A = ad - bc\). It is the factor by which areas grow or shrink under the transformation: \(\det = 2\) doubles every area, \(\det = 1\) preserves it, and a negative determinant flips orientation (like a mirror). When \(\det A = 0\) the grid has been squashed onto a line — a dimension is lost, information is destroyed, and the matrix has no inverse.

media.caption: The shaded unit square's area equals |det A|.

cards.deploy: A one-number test for whether a transformation is reversible, and by how much it expands or shrinks.
cards.counter: A large determinant doesn't mean a matrix is 'well-behaved' for computation; a separate measure (the condition number) governs numerical reliability.

quiz.q: If det A = 0, the transformation…

cards.title: Eigenvectors: the directions that don't turn
cards.fact: An eigenvector is a direction a transformation only stretches — it never rotates it.
cards.detail: Under a matrix \(A\), most vectors swing off to a new direction. A special few hold their direction and are merely scaled: \(A\vec v = \lambda\vec v\). Such a \(\vec v\) is an eigenvector, and the stretch factor \(\lambda\) is its eigenvalue. These reveal a transformation's natural axes — the skeleton it acts along. Google's original PageRank found an eigenvector of the web's link matrix; principal component analysis finds the eigenvectors of data to compress it.

media.say: A times v equals lambda times v — the matrix only stretches v by the factor lambda.
media.caption: Same direction, scaled by λ.
Look for an arrow that stays on its own line — that's an eigenvector.

cards.deploy: Finds the hidden axes of a transformation or dataset — behind PCA, PageRank, and stability analysis.
cards.counter: Not every real matrix has real eigenvectors — a pure rotation turns every direction, so its eigenvalues are complex numbers, with no real axis it leaves alone.

quiz.q: For an eigenvector v of A, Av equals…

cards.title: Probability: a number from 0 to 1
cards.fact: A probability scores how likely something is, from 0 (never) to 1 (certain).
cards.detail: List everything that could happen — the 'sample space'. If each outcome is equally likely, the probability of an event is just the share that counts as a success: \(P(A) = \frac{\text{favourable outcomes}}{\text{all outcomes}}\). A fair die has six faces, so \(P(\text{roll a 4}) = \tfrac{1}{6}\). 0 means impossible, 1 means certain, and 0.5 is an even chance. Everything else in probability builds on this.

media.caption: A fair die: six equally likely outcomes, each 1/6.

cards.deploy: Turns vague talk of 'likely' and 'rare' into a number you can compare and combine.
cards.counter: The 'equally likely' shortcut only works for symmetric setups like dice; for real events (rain tomorrow) probability means a long-run frequency or a degree of belief — a split between the frequentist and Bayesian schools.

quiz.q: A probability of 1 means an event is…

cards.title: Adding and multiplying probabilities
cards.fact: Use OR to add chances, AND to multiply them.
cards.detail: For the chance of A or B, add — then subtract the overlap so it isn't counted twice: \(P(A\text{ or }B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A\text{ and }B)\). For A and B both happening, multiply — and if they're independent (one doesn't affect the other), it's simply \(P(A\text{ and }B) = P(A)\,P(B)\). Two fair coins both landing heads: \(\tfrac12 \times \tfrac12 = \tfrac14\).

media.say: the chance of both, when neither affects the other, is the two chances multiplied.
media.caption: Independent events: multiply.
Two fair coins: each combination is ½ × ½ = ¼.

cards.deploy: Lets you build the odds of complex events from simple ones.
cards.counter: The multiply rule fails when events are linked: P(rain) and P(I carry an umbrella) aren't independent, so multiplying understates the truth.

quiz.q: For two independent events, P(A and B) equals…

cards.title: Conditional probability: given that…
cards.fact: The probability of A changes once you know B has happened.
cards.detail: Written \(P(A \mid B)\) — 'the probability of A given B' — it narrows the world to the cases where B is true: \(P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A\text{ and }B)}{P(B)}\). Knowing it rained (B) changes the chance the ground is wet (A). When \(P(A \mid B) = P(A)\), knowing B told you nothing — that's exactly what independence means.

media.plain: P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B)
media.say: the chance of A given B is the chance of both, divided by the chance of B.
media.caption: Restrict the world to the cases where B happened.
Knowing it rained lifts the chance the ground is wet.

cards.deploy: The formal way to update a probability when new information arrives.
cards.counter: People routinely confuse P(A|B) with P(B|A) — the 'prosecutor's fallacy'; the chance of a match given innocence is not the chance of innocence given a match.

quiz.q: P(A | B) is read as…

cards.title: Bayes' theorem: updating beliefs with evidence
cards.fact: Bayes' rule flips a conditional probability — turning a test result into an updated belief.
cards.detail: It connects \(P(H \mid E)\) (a hypothesis given the evidence) to \(P(E \mid H)\) (the evidence given the hypothesis): \(P(H \mid E) = \frac{P(E \mid H)\,P(H)}{P(E)}\). The starting belief \(P(H)\) is the 'prior'; the answer \(P(H \mid E)\) is the 'posterior'. Its sting is the base rate: a 99%-accurate test for a disease that 1 in 1000 people have still gives mostly false alarms, because healthy people vastly outnumber sick ones.

media.say: the updated belief is the evidence's likelihood times the prior, divided by how likely the evidence was overall.
media.caption: Prior belief × evidence → updated (posterior) belief.
A rare disease (1%): even a positive test leaves you far from certain.

cards.deploy: The engine of rational updating — and of spam filters, medical screening and Bayesian machine learning.
cards.counter: Bayesians treat the prior as a real degree of belief to be updated; frequentists object that priors are subjective. The maths is agreed; what a probability *means* is not.

quiz.q: In Bayes' theorem, the starting belief P(H) before seeing evidence is the…

cards.title: Random variables: numbers from chance
cards.fact: A random variable attaches a number to each uncertain outcome.
cards.detail: Call it \(X\). For one die roll, \(X\) is the face shown; for a coin, you might set heads \(= 1\), tails \(= 0\). A discrete random variable takes separate values (0, 1, 2…); a continuous one can be any value in a range (a height, a wait time). Its 'distribution' lists how much probability sits on each value — the bridge from single outcomes to averages and spread.
cards.deploy: Lets you do arithmetic — averages, sums, spreads — on the outcomes of chance.
cards.counter: The number you assign is a modelling choice: coding categories as 1, 2, 3 can smuggle in a false sense that the gaps between them are equal.

quiz.q: A random variable that can take any value in a range is…

cards.title: Expected value: the long-run average
cards.fact: The expected value is the average you'd get from many repeats — each outcome weighted by its probability.
cards.detail: Multiply each value by its probability and add: \(E[X] = \sum_i x_i\,p_i\). A fair die's expected roll is \(\tfrac16(1+2+\dots+6) = 3.5\) — a value you can never actually roll, but the long-run average. It's the foundation of fair prices, insurance and betting: a bet is 'fair' when its expected gain is zero.

media.say: the expected value is each outcome times its probability, all added up.
media.caption: Each outcome, weighted by how likely it is.

cards.deploy: The single best summary of a random quantity — and the thing rational decisions try to maximise.
cards.counter: Expected value ignores risk: a 1-in-a-million shot at a billion has a high expectation, but few would stake their house on it. That gap is why utility, not raw money, often guides choices.

quiz.q: The expected value of a fair six-sided die is…

cards.title: Variance and standard deviation: the spread
cards.fact: Variance measures how far outcomes typically stray from the average.
cards.detail: Take each value's distance from the mean \(\mu\), square it (so positives and negatives don't cancel), and average: \(\sigma^2 = E[(X-\mu)^2]\). The standard deviation \(\sigma = \sqrt{\sigma^2}\) brings it back to the original units. Two classes can share a mean score of 60 yet feel completely different — one tightly bunched, the other spread from 20 to 95. That difference is the standard deviation.

media.say: variance is the average squared distance from the mean.
media.caption: Square the distances from the mean, then average.
Same mean, different spread: σ sets the width.

cards.deploy: Quantifies risk, noise and consistency — the second number (after the mean) you reach for.
cards.counter: Squaring makes variance hypersensitive to outliers; a single freak value can dominate it, which is why robust measures (like the interquartile range) are sometimes preferred.

quiz.q: The standard deviation is the…

cards.title: Distributions: uniform, Bernoulli, binomial
cards.fact: A distribution is the shape of how probability is spread across outcomes.
cards.detail: A few shapes recur everywhere. The uniform puts equal weight on each outcome (a fair die). The Bernoulli is a single yes/no trial with success probability \(p\) (one coin flip). The binomial counts successes in \(n\) independent trials — flip 4 coins and the number of heads follows it, peaking in the middle. Recognising the shape tells you what to expect.

media.caption: Heads in 4 coin flips (binomial): the middle is likeliest.

cards.deploy: Names the common patterns so you can pick the right model instead of starting from scratch.
cards.counter: Reaching for a textbook distribution can impose a shape the data doesn't have — real counts are often more skewed or heavy-tailed than the binomial or normal assume.

quiz.q: The number of heads in several independent coin flips follows the…

cards.title: The normal (Gaussian) distribution
cards.fact: The bell curve: a smooth hump set by just two numbers — its mean and its spread.
cards.detail: The normal distribution's density is \(f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\,e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}\). The mean \(\mu\) slides the peak left or right; the standard deviation \(\sigma\) makes it wide or narrow. About 68% of values land within one \(\sigma\) of the mean, 95% within two. It appears so often because sums of many small independent effects tend toward it — the reason it underpins so much of statistics.

media.caption: Slide μ to move the peak, σ to widen or narrow it.

cards.deploy: The default model for measurement error, natural variation and sample averages.
cards.counter: Assuming normality is dangerous in the tails: finance learned in 2008 that 'impossible' extreme moves happen far more often than the bell curve allows (fat tails).

quiz.q: Two numbers fully define a normal distribution: the mean and the…

cards.title: Mean, median, and mode
cards.fact: Three ways to name the 'typical' value — and they can tell different stories.
cards.detail: The mean is the arithmetic average (add up, divide by how many). The median is the middle value when sorted. The mode is the most common value. They agree for symmetric data, but a few extreme values pull the mean while leaving the median put: most people earn below the mean income, because a handful of huge earners drag the average up. The median is the fairer 'typical' there.
