media.caption: A long right tail (like incomes) drags the mean past the median.

cards.deploy: The first summary of any dataset — and choosing mean vs median can change the headline.
cards.counter: Any single number hides the shape: the same mean can describe steady data or wildly volatile data. Always ask about spread too.

quiz.q: For incomes with a few very high earners, the 'typical' value is best given by the…

cards.title: Population vs sample: estimating from a piece
cards.fact: Statistics infers the whole from a part — and a biased part lies.
cards.detail: You rarely measure everyone (the 'population'), so you take a 'sample' and estimate. The catch is sampling error: any sample differs from the whole by chance, and that wobble shrinks roughly as \(1/\sqrt{n}\) — to halve the error you need four times the data. Worse than random error is bias: a sample that systematically over-represents some group. The 1936 Literary Digest poll surveyed millions yet called the US election wrongly, because its phone-and-car owners skewed wealthy.
cards.deploy: The basis of all polling, testing and science: how to learn about the many from the few.
cards.counter: A bigger sample cuts random error but not bias — a huge skewed sample is confidently wrong. Size is no substitute for representativeness.

quiz.q: To halve a sample's random error, you roughly need to…

cards.title: Hypothesis testing and the p-value
cards.fact: A p-value asks: if nothing were going on, how surprising would this data be?
cards.detail: Start with a 'null hypothesis' — no effect. The p-value is the probability of seeing data at least this extreme if the null were true. A small p (often \(p < 0.05\)) means the data would be surprising under 'no effect', so researchers reject the null. It does not give the probability that the hypothesis is true, nor the size or importance of an effect.

media.tex: p = P(\text{data this extreme} \mid \text{null is true})
media.plain: p = P(data this extreme | null hypothesis true)
media.say: the p-value is the chance of data this extreme, assuming nothing is going on.
media.caption: Small p → the data is surprising if there's really no effect.

cards.deploy: The standard gatekeeper for 'is this result more than noise?' across the sciences.
cards.counter: The American Statistical Association warned in 2016 that p-values are widely misused: p < 0.05 is an arbitrary line, says nothing about effect size, and 'p-hacking' can manufacture it. A small p is not proof.

quiz.q: A small p-value means the data would be… if the null hypothesis were true.

cards.title: Confidence intervals: the margin of error
cards.fact: A confidence interval reports a range for an estimate, not a single false-precise number.
cards.detail: Rather than '52% support', a poll says '52% ± 3%'. The 95% confidence interval is built so that, across many repeated samples, about 95% of such intervals would contain the true value. A wider interval means more uncertainty; more data narrows it. It keeps you honest about how much the single estimate could be off.
cards.deploy: Communicates uncertainty alongside an estimate — essential for reading polls and studies.
cards.counter: The 95% refers to the long-run behaviour of the method, not to one interval: it's wrong to say 'there's a 95% chance the truth is in this particular range' — a subtlety frequentists stress and Bayesians sidestep with credible intervals.

quiz.q: A wider confidence interval indicates…

cards.title: Least-squares regression: the best-fit line
cards.fact: Regression draws the straight line that comes closest to a cloud of points.
cards.detail: Fit a straight line \(\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\) — an intercept and a slope — through a cloud of points. The standard method is ordinary least squares (OLS): pick the line that makes the total squared vertical gap between the points and the line as small as possible, \(\sum_i (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\). Why square the gaps rather than just add them up? Squaring punishes big misses far more than small ones and — crucially — leaves exactly one best line. The fitted slope \(\beta_1\) then estimates how much \(y\) rises per unit of \(x\). It is the workhorse of empirical science and the simplest machine-learning model there is.

media.caption: The line that minimises the total squared gap to the points.

cards.deploy: The standard tool for measuring how one quantity moves with another, and predicting from it.
cards.counter: A fitted line can mislead: it assumes a straight relationship, is dragged by outliers, and — as the correlation/causation card warns — a good fit never proves x causes y.

quiz.q: Least-squares regression chooses the line that minimises the total…
choices: Squared vertical distance to the points

cards.title: Machine learning: fitting a function to data
cards.fact: Instead of writing the rule by hand, you let the machine find a function that fits examples.
cards.detail: A model is a function \(f\) with adjustable numbers inside it, called parameters (or weights). 'Training' means tuning those numbers until \(f\) maps inputs to the right outputs on example data — learning the rule from cases rather than being told it. Show it thousands of labelled photos and it adjusts its weights until it separates cats from dogs. The input is a vector of features; the output is a prediction.

media.caption: Learning = finding the function that best fits the examples.

cards.deploy: The core idea behind modern AI: learn the function from data instead of programming it.
cards.counter: A model only learns patterns present in its training data — including the biases and gaps in that data, which it will faithfully reproduce and even amplify.

quiz.q: In machine learning, 'training' adjusts a model's…

cards.title: Linear regression as your first model
cards.fact: Predict with a weighted sum of the inputs: ŷ = w·x + b.
cards.detail: Give each input feature a weight, multiply, add them up, and add a bias: \(\hat{y} = \vec{w}\cdot\vec{x} + b\). That dot product is the whole model — a price predicted from size, location and age is just their weighted sum. 'Learning' means finding the weights \(\vec{w}\) and bias \(b\) that fit the data best, by making the error as small as possible. With a handful of features you can solve for them exactly with ordinary least squares; with millions you instead descend the error surface step by step (gradient descent) — both routes chase the same minimum. Simple, fast, and the template every fancier model extends.

media.say: the prediction is the weights dotted with the inputs, plus a bias.
media.caption: A prediction is a weighted sum of the features.
One feature: the model is just the best-fit line.

cards.deploy: The clearest place to see what 'a model' and 'weights' actually mean before things get deep.
cards.counter: A straight weighted sum can't capture curves or interactions; its honesty about that limit is also why it rarely overfits and stays easy to interpret.

quiz.q: In ŷ = w·x + b, the vector w holds the…

cards.title: The loss function: scoring how wrong you are
cards.fact: A loss function turns 'how bad is this model?' into a single number to minimise.
cards.detail: Compare each prediction \(\hat{y}_i\) to the truth \(y_i\), and summarise the misses in one number. The common choice for regression is the mean squared error: \(L = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i (\hat{y}_i - y_i)^2\). Squaring punishes big mistakes harder and keeps the loss positive. Training becomes a clear goal: choose the weights that make this number as small as possible.

media.say: the loss is the average of the squared gaps between prediction and truth.
media.caption: Mean squared error: average of the squared misses.
Loss as the weight changes: a valley to roll into.

cards.deploy: Defines 'best' precisely, so training is just minimising one number.
cards.counter: The loss you pick is a value judgement: squared error chases outliers, while other losses (absolute error, cross-entropy) reward different behaviour — optimise the wrong loss and you get the wrong model.

quiz.q: Mean squared error squares the errors mainly to…
choices: Punish big mistakes more and stay positive

cards.title: Gradient descent: rolling downhill to the best fit
cards.fact: Take small steps in the downhill direction of the loss until you reach the bottom.
cards.detail: The gradient \(\nabla L\) points uphill on the loss surface, so step the opposite way: \(\vec{w} \leftarrow \vec{w} - \eta\,\nabla L\). The learning rate \(\eta\) sets the step size — too small and training crawls, too large and it overshoots and diverges. Repeat, and the weights roll down into a valley of low loss. This one rule trains almost every model in modern machine learning.

layers.body: The gradient \(\nabla L\) points uphill on the loss surface, so step the opposite way: \(\vec{w} \leftarrow \vec{w} - \eta\,\nabla L\). The learning rate \(\eta\) sets the step size — too small and training crawls, too large and it overshoots and diverges. Repeat, and the weights roll down into a valley of low loss. This one rule trains almost every model in modern machine learning.

Say the loss is \(L(w)=(w-3)^2\), so its slope is \(L'(w)=2(w-3)\). Start at \(w=0\) with learning rate \(\eta=0.1\).

Step 1: slope \(=2(0-3)=-6\), so \(w \leftarrow 0-0.1\times(-6)=0.6\). Step 2: slope \(=-4.8\), so \(w \leftarrow 1.08\). Step 3: \(w\approx1.46\)… each step slides \(w\) toward 3, where the slope is 0 — the bottom. Pick \(\eta=1.1\) instead and the steps overshoot and blow up.

media.say: new weights equal old weights minus the learning rate times the uphill gradient.
media.caption: Step against the gradient — downhill on the loss.
Press step: the ball rolls toward the minimum. Try a big η.

cards.deploy: The universal training algorithm — understand this and you understand how models learn.
cards.counter: On a bumpy, non-convex loss it can stall in a local dip or a saddle far from the best solution; momentum and adaptive methods (like Adam) are patches for that, not cures.

quiz.q: Gradient descent updates weights by stepping…

cards.title: Logistic regression and the sigmoid
cards.fact: Squash a weighted sum through an S-curve to get a probability between 0 and 1.
cards.detail: For yes/no questions you want a probability, not an unbounded number. The sigmoid \(\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}\) takes any value and bends it into the range 0 to 1: large positive \(z\) → near 1, large negative → near 0, zero → exactly 0.5. Feed it the weighted sum \(z = \vec{w}\cdot\vec{x} + b\) and you have logistic regression — a classifier that outputs calibrated probabilities.

media.caption: The sigmoid squashes any number into a 0–1 probability.

cards.deploy: The standard way to turn a score into a probability — and the classic activation in a neuron.
cards.counter: Its probabilities are only as honest as the model: a confident sigmoid output can still be badly miscalibrated if the features or data are skewed.

quiz.q: The sigmoid function maps any input to a value between…

cards.title: The artificial neuron
cards.fact: A neuron weighs its inputs, adds them up, and fires through an activation function.
cards.detail: The basic unit: take inputs \(\vec{x}\), weight and sum them with a bias, then pass the result through a non-linear activation: \(y = \sigma(\vec{w}\cdot\vec{x} + b)\). The weighted sum is a dot product; the activation (a sigmoid, or today usually a ReLU) lets the unit bend, not just draw a straight line. One neuron is a tiny logistic regression — the Lego brick everything bigger is built from.

media.say: the output is the activation of the weighted sum of inputs plus a bias.
media.caption: Weigh, sum, then squash: one artificial neuron.
Three weighted inputs feed one neuron.

cards.deploy: The atom of neural networks — every deep model is millions of these wired together.
cards.counter: The brain analogy is loose marketing: a biological neuron is vastly more complex, and this unit is better understood as a tunable mathematical function than as a model of a cell.

quiz.q: An artificial neuron applies an activation function to the…
choices: Weighted sum of inputs plus bias

cards.title: A neural network: layers of neurons
cards.fact: Stack neurons into layers and a network becomes matrices squashed through activations.
cards.detail: A layer computes many neurons at once: collect their weights into a matrix \(W\) and the whole layer is \(\vec{h} = \sigma(W\vec{x} + \vec{b})\) — a matrix-vector product, then an activation, applied entry by entry. Stack layers and the output of one feeds the next. Without the non-linear activations the stack would collapse into a single linear map; with them, the network can approximate almost any function. This is deep learning's core.

layers.body: A layer computes many neurons at once: collect their weights into a matrix \(W\) and the whole layer is \(\vec{h} = \sigma(W\vec{x} + \vec{b})\) — a matrix-vector product, then an activation, applied entry by entry. Stack layers and the output of one feeds the next. Without the non-linear activations the stack would collapse into a single linear map; with them, the network can approximate almost any function. This is deep learning's core.

Take one layer with 2 inputs feeding 3 neurons. The weights form a \(3\times2\) matrix \(W\); the inputs are a length-2 vector \(\vec x\). Then \(W\vec x\) is length-3 (one weighted sum per neuron), you add a length-3 bias \(\vec b\), and squash each of the 3 entries.

So '3 neurons on 2 inputs' is exactly: multiply by a \(3\times2\) matrix, add 3 numbers, squash 3 numbers. The next layer takes those 3 outputs as its own inputs — another matrix, another squash.

media.say: a layer is the activation of a matrix times the inputs, plus a bias vector.
media.caption: One layer: a matrix multiply, a bias, then a squash.
Inputs flow through hidden layers to outputs — every arrow is a weight.

cards.deploy: Explains why linear algebra and calculus are the language of AI: a net is matrices and activations composed.
cards.counter: 'Can approximate any function' is an existence result, not a recipe — it says nothing about how much data, compute, or luck it takes to actually find the right weights.

quiz.q: A neural-network layer is essentially a matrix multiply followed by…

cards.title: Backpropagation: the chain rule that trains the net
cards.fact: Backprop sends the error backwards through the layers to find every weight's gradient.
cards.detail: Gradient descent needs the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight — and a deep net has millions. Backpropagation computes them all efficiently by applying the chain rule layer by layer, from the output error back toward the input. Each layer passes the blame for the error to the one before it. It's just the chain rule, organised — and its rediscovery in the 1980s is what made training deep networks practical.

layers.body: Gradient descent needs the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight — and a deep net has millions. Backpropagation computes them all efficiently by applying the chain rule layer by layer, from the output error back toward the input. Each layer passes the blame for the error to the one before it. It's just the chain rule, organised — and its rediscovery in the 1980s is what made training deep networks practical.

Chain one neuron: \(z=wx\), then \(a=\sigma(z)\), then loss \(L=(a-y)^2\). To adjust \(w\), multiply the rates along the chain:

\(\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial w}=\underbrace{2(a-y)}_{\text{loss}\to a}\cdot\underbrace{\sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))}_{a\to z}\cdot\underbrace{x}_{z\to w}\).

Each layer passes that running product back to the layer before it — backprop just does this for every weight at once, output-side first.

media.say: a weight's effect on the loss is the chain of how it changes the output, times how that changes the loss.
media.caption: The chain rule, applied backwards through every layer.
Training sends the error backward, right to left, tuning every weight.

cards.deploy: The reason deep networks are trainable at all — the algorithm that powers the whole field.
cards.counter: Backprop finds gradients, not good solutions: it can suffer vanishing or exploding gradients in deep stacks, which architectures (ReLUs, residual connections, normalisation) were invented to tame.

quiz.q: Backpropagation is fundamentally an application of the…

cards.title: Softmax and cross-entropy
cards.fact: Softmax turns a list of scores into probabilities that sum to 1; cross-entropy scores how good they are.
cards.detail: For many classes, softmax exponentiates each score and divides by the total: \(\text{softmax}(z)_i = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}}\). The biggest score gets the most probability, but all stay positive and sum to 1. Cross-entropy then measures the gap from the true label — heavily punishing confident wrong answers via the logarithm. Together they are the standard output and loss for classification, from image labels to the next-word predictions of a language model.

media.say: each score is exponentiated, then divided by the total — giving probabilities that add to one.
media.caption: Scores in, probabilities (summing to 1) out.
Raw scores → softmax probabilities that sum to 1.

cards.deploy: The standard final layer of a classifier — including the token probabilities an LLM samples from.
cards.counter: Softmax always returns a confident-looking distribution even on nonsense input; it never says 'none of the above', which is one root of AI models' overconfidence.

quiz.q: Softmax converts a list of scores into…

cards.title: Overfitting and the bias–variance trade-off
cards.fact: A model that memorises its training data can fail completely on new data.
cards.detail: Push a model hard enough and it fits the training points perfectly — including their noise. That's overfitting: low error on data it has seen, high error on data it hasn't. The opposite, underfitting, is a model too simple to catch the real pattern. This is the bias–variance trade-off: too simple misses the signal (bias), too flexible chases the noise (variance). You judge a model on held-out test data, and rein in flexibility with regularisation.

media.caption: The simple straight line generalises; a wiggly curve through every point would not.

cards.deploy: The central discipline of machine learning: build models that generalise, not memorise.
cards.counter: More data and bigger models complicate the neat trade-off — very large networks can fit noise yet still generalise ('double descent'), a phenomenon classical theory didn't predict.

quiz.q: A model with low training error but high test error is…

cards.title: Attention and transformers: the maths behind LLMs
cards.fact: Attention lets each word pull in the others most relevant to it — by dot products and softmax.
cards.detail: A transformer represents each token as a vector and lets tokens look at one another. Each forms a query \(Q\), key \(K\) and value \(V\). The relevance of one token to another is their dot product (alignment); softmax turns those scores into weights that sum to 1; the output is the weighted blend of values: \(\text{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d}}\right)V\). Stacked in layers, this is the architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017) behind GPT and modern large language models.

layers.body: A transformer represents each token as a vector and lets tokens look at one another. Each forms a query \(Q\), key \(K\) and value \(V\). The relevance of one token to another is their dot product (alignment); softmax turns those scores into weights that sum to 1; the output is the weighted blend of values: \(\text{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d}}\right)V\). Stacked in layers, this is the architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017) behind GPT and modern large language models.

Three words, each with a query, key and value vector. To refresh word 3, score its query against every key with a dot product — say \(q_3\!\cdot\!k_1=2,\ q_3\!\cdot\!k_2=0,\ q_3\!\cdot\!k_3=4\).

Softmax turns \((2,0,4)\) into weights that sum to 1 — about \((0.11,0.02,0.87)\). The new word-3 vector is that weighted blend of the value vectors: mostly \(v_3\), a little \(v_1\). Score by similarity, soften into weights, mix the values.

media.say: score every pair by a dot product, soften the scores into weights, then blend the values.
media.caption: Dot-product similarity → softmax weights → weighted mix of values.
Attention weights: how much the blank word draws on each earlier word.

cards.deploy: Connects the whole maths ladder to today's AI: dot products, softmax and matrices are literally how an LLM reads.
cards.counter: Attention shows which tokens a model weighted, not why, and not whether it 'understands' — reading attention maps as explanations of a model's reasoning is contested (Jain & Wallace, 2019).

quiz.q: The core similarity score inside attention is computed with a…

cards.title: A dollar today beats a dollar tomorrow
cards.fact: Money now is worth more than the same money later, because it can be invested to grow.
cards.detail: Put a present value \(PV\) in at interest rate \(r\), and after \(n\) years it grows to \(FV = PV(1+r)^n\). At 5% a year, $100 today becomes \(100\times1.05 = 105\) next year — so a promise of $105 next year is worth only $100 now. Timing changes value. This one idea sits under every loan, investment, mortgage and valuation in finance.

media.say: future value is the present value times one-plus-the-rate, compounded for n years.
media.caption: Money today grows at rate r over n years.

cards.deploy: The root of interest, discounting and every 'what is it worth today?' calculation.
cards.counter: It assumes you can actually earn that rate safely; with negative real rates or high inflation, 'more later' can be worth less in real terms — the logic can invert.

quiz.q: Why is money today worth more than the same amount next year?
choices: It can be invested to grow

cards.title: Compound interest: interest on interest
cards.fact: Compounding pays interest on your interest, so growth feeds on itself and snowballs.
cards.detail: Simple interest pays only on the original sum. Compound interest pays on the sum plus all the interest earned so far, so it grows exponentially: \(FV = PV(1+r)^n\). The 'Rule of 72' is the handy shortcut — money doubles in roughly \(72/r\) years (about 12 years at 6%). Over decades the gap between simple and compound growth becomes huge, which is why starting to save early matters far more than saving a little extra later.

media.caption: Same 7% rate over 30 years: compound (curve) pulls away from simple (line).

cards.deploy: Explains why long-horizon saving, and long-horizon debt, both balloon.
cards.counter: Compounding cuts both ways: the same maths that builds a pension turns a 20%-APR credit-card balance into a trap. It rewards savers and punishes borrowers identically.

quiz.q: By the Rule of 72, money at 6% a year doubles in about…

cards.title: Present value: discounting the future
cards.fact: Present value runs compounding backwards — what is future money worth today?
cards.detail: Discounting is the reverse of compounding. To value \(FV\) received in \(n\) years, divide by the growth factor: \(PV = \frac{FV}{(1+r)^n}\). Here \(r\) is the 'discount rate' — your required return or cost of capital. A higher discount rate shrinks the value of distant cash, which is exactly why rising interest rates hit long-dated bonds and growth stocks hardest: most of their value sits far in the future.

media.say: present value is the future amount divided by one-plus-the-rate, n times over.
media.caption: Discount future money back to today.
The discount factor: a dollar far in the future is worth little today.

cards.deploy: The core move in valuing anything that pays off over time — bonds, projects, companies.
cards.counter: The answer is only as good as the chosen \(r\): small changes in the discount rate swing long-term valuations wildly, so 'what's it worth' is often really a hidden argument about \(r\).

quiz.q: Raising the discount rate makes the present value of future cash…

cards.title: NPV and IRR: is an investment worth it?
cards.fact: NPV sums an investment's discounted cash flows; IRR is the rate at which it breaks even.
cards.detail: A project throws off cash \(CF_t\) over the years. Net present value discounts each back to today and adds them up, minus the upfront cost \(C_0\): \(NPV = \sum_t \frac{CF_t}{(1+r)^t} - C_0\). If \(NPV > 0\), the project beats your discount rate, so take it. The internal rate of return (IRR) is the special rate that makes \(NPV = 0\) — the project's own break-even return. Together they are finance's standard 'should we do this?' test.

media.say: net present value is every future cash flow discounted to today and summed, minus the upfront cost.
media.caption: Discount every cash flow, add them, subtract the cost.

cards.deploy: The decision rule for capital projects, acquisitions and big purchases.
cards.counter: IRR misleads when cash flows change sign more than once (it can have several values) or when ranking projects of different size; Brealey & Myers' standard text argues NPV is the sounder rule.

quiz.q: A project should be accepted (on the NPV rule) when its NPV is…

cards.title: Risk and return: no free lunch
cards.fact: Higher expected return is the reward for bearing more risk — you rarely get one without the other.
cards.detail: An asset's return is uncertain, so we summarise it with two numbers: the expected return (its mean \(\mu\)) and its risk (the standard deviation of returns \(\sigma\), called volatility). Treasury bills offer low \(\mu\) and low \(\sigma\); stocks offer higher \(\mu\) but a bumpier \(\sigma\). The extra expected return for taking on risk is the 'risk premium'. Plot \(\mu\) against \(\sigma\) and you see the trade-off every investor faces.

media.caption: Risk (σ, across) vs expected return (up): more of one tends to mean more of the other.

cards.deploy: The mental model behind every portfolio choice: what return am I paid for this risk?
cards.counter: The neat trade-off assumes investors are rational and that risk is fully captured by σ; behavioural economists (Kahneman, Thaler) show people feel losses about twice as hard as gains, so real 'risk' isn't symmetric.

quiz.q: In finance, an asset's 'volatility' usually refers to its…

cards.title: Diversification: the only free lunch
cards.fact: Combining assets that don't move together cuts risk without cutting expected return.
cards.detail: Mix two assets and the portfolio's expected return is just the weighted average — but its risk is not. Variances combine through correlation: \(\sigma_p^2 = w_1^2\sigma_1^2 + w_2^2\sigma_2^2 + 2w_1 w_2\,\rho\,\sigma_1\sigma_2\). When the correlation \(\rho\) is low or negative, that last cross term shrinks the total. Harry Markowitz (1952) built modern portfolio theory on this: spreading across uncorrelated assets is the closest thing to a free lunch in finance.

media.say: portfolio variance is each asset's weighted variance plus a cross term that shrinks when the correlation rho is low.
media.caption: Low correlation ρ shrinks the cross term — and the risk.

cards.deploy: The mathematical case for not betting everything on one stock, sector or country.
cards.counter: It only removes asset-specific risk; market-wide ('systematic') risk stays. Worse, in a crash correlations jump toward 1 — so diversification fails exactly when it's needed most (2008).

quiz.q: Diversification reduces a portfolio's risk most when the assets' returns are…

cards.title: CAPM: pricing risk with beta
cards.fact: An asset should be paid a return for its market risk — measured by beta — and nothing for risk you could diversify away.
cards.detail: Since diversification removes asset-specific risk, only market risk deserves a reward. The Capital Asset Pricing Model sets expected return as the risk-free rate plus a premium proportional to beta: \(E[R] = R_f + \beta\,(E[R_m] - R_f)\). Beta measures how strongly the asset swings with the market: \(\beta = 1\) moves with it, \(\beta > 1\) amplifies it, \(\beta < 1\) dampens it. William Sharpe won a Nobel for it, and it is still the workhorse for estimating the 'cost of equity'.

media.say: expected return is the risk-free rate plus beta times the market's excess return.
media.caption: More market risk (beta) earns more expected return.
The security market line: expected return rises with beta.

cards.deploy: The standard way to turn 'how risky is this?' into a required return for valuing a company.
cards.counter: Empirically, beta predicts returns poorly. Fama & French (1992) showed company size and value explain more, and many quants treat single-factor CAPM as a teaching model rather than how markets really price risk.

quiz.q: In CAPM, an asset with beta greater than 1…

cards.title: The efficient-market hypothesis
cards.fact: If prices already reflect all known information, you can't reliably beat the market.
cards.detail: Eugene Fama's efficient-market hypothesis (1970) holds that prices instantly absorb available information, so consistent outperformance is impossible without luck or inside knowledge. It comes in strengths: 'weak' (past prices don't predict future ones), 'semi-strong' (all public news is already priced in), and 'strong' (even private information is). It is the central argument for cheap, passive index funds over costly stock-picking.
cards.deploy: The case for index investing — and a sharp test to apply to anyone promising to beat the market.
cards.counter: Robert Shiller (who shared the 2013 Nobel with Fama) argues markets show 'excess volatility' and psychology-driven bubbles; the dot-com and 2008 housing manias look hard to square with efficiency. Fama's efficiency versus Shiller's behavioural view remains an open dispute.

quiz.q: The efficient-market hypothesis implies that beating the market consistently is…
choices: Very hard without luck or inside information

cards.title: Random walks: why prices resist prediction
cards.fact: If today's price already holds all information, tomorrow's move depends on tomorrow's news — which is random.
cards.detail: When prices reflect what's known, the next change is driven by the next surprise, so prices wander like a 'random walk': each step is a random shock added to the last. Finance models this as geometric Brownian motion — the continuous-time random walk underneath option pricing. Burton Malkiel popularised the provocation that a blindfolded monkey throwing darts could pick stocks about as well as many professionals.
cards.deploy: Explains why short-term price forecasts and most 'technical' chart-reading fail to beat chance.
cards.counter: Pure randomness is an idealisation: documented momentum and mean-reversion effects, and the fat-tailed jumps Benoit Mandelbrot and Nassim Taleb emphasise, mean real prices are not a tidy Gaussian random walk.

quiz.q: A 'random walk' in prices means the next change is mostly…

cards.title: Options: the right, not the obligation
cards.fact: An option is the right — but not the duty — to buy or sell at a fixed price.
cards.detail: A call option lets you buy an asset at a fixed 'strike' price \(K\); a put lets you sell at \(K\). You exercise only if it pays. A call's payoff at expiry is \(\max(0,\ S - K)\), where \(S\) is the market price: worthless if \(S < K\), then climbing one-for-one above \(K\) — the famous 'hockey stick'. Options let you hedge a risk or speculate with a capped, known downside: the premium you paid.

media.caption: A call's payoff vs price S: flat until the strike K, then a 45° climb.

cards.deploy: The building block of hedging and of every structured payoff in modern markets.
cards.counter: The capped downside is sold by someone with uncapped risk: option sellers can lose far more than any premium, as 2008 and the 2021 meme-stock squeezes showed.

quiz.q: A call option's payoff at expiry is max(0, S − K). If S is below the strike K, the payoff is…

cards.title: Black–Scholes: pricing an option
cards.fact: A formula prices an option using the bell curve and the idea that you can hedge it perfectly.
cards.detail: Fischer Black, Myron Scholes and Robert Merton (1973) found the fair value of a call before expiry. It blends the stock price, strike, time, interest rate and volatility, weighting outcomes by the normal distribution: \(C = S\,N(d_1) - K e^{-rt} N(d_2)\), where \(N(\cdot)\) is the normal cumulative probability. The deep insight: you can replicate an option by continuously rebalancing stock and cash, so no-arbitrage pins down its price. It won the 1997 Nobel and launched the modern derivatives industry.

media.say: the call value is the stock weighted by a normal probability, minus the discounted strike weighted by another.
media.caption: Outcomes weighted by the normal curve N(·).
Black–Scholes weights future outcomes by the normal (Gaussian) curve.

cards.deploy: The foundation of derivatives pricing — and a clean example of the no-arbitrage idea.
cards.counter: Its assumptions — constant volatility, no jumps, a Gaussian world — break in crises: 1987 and 2008 revealed far fatter tails, and the market's 'volatility smile' prices in exactly what the formula omits. LTCM's 1998 collapse, with Scholes and Merton aboard, is the cautionary tale.

quiz.q: The Black–Scholes formula weights outcomes using which distribution?

cards.title: Bonds: price and yield seesaw
cards.fact: A bond's price and its yield always move in opposite directions.
cards.detail: A bond pays fixed coupons plus its face value at maturity, so its price is the present value of those cash flows: \(P = \sum_t \frac{CF_t}{(1+y)^t}\). Because \(y\) sits in the denominator, a higher yield means a lower price — they are locked on a seesaw. 'Duration' measures how sharp the seesaw is: long-dated bonds swing far more when yields move, which is why a rate rise punishes 30-year bonds much harder than 2-year ones.

media.caption: Bond price falls (and convexly) as the yield rises.

cards.deploy: The key to reading the bond market and why central-bank rate moves ripple through everything.
cards.counter: The seesaw is exact only for default-free bonds held to maturity; credit risk, inflation and call features complicate it — 2022's bond rout caught many who underestimated how hard duration bites.

quiz.q: When market yields rise, existing bond prices generally…

cards.title: Leverage and tail risk
cards.fact: Borrowing to invest magnifies gains and losses alike — and can wipe you out entirely.
cards.detail: Leverage means investing with borrowed money. Put in $1 of your own plus $9 borrowed, and a 10% gain on the $10 doubles your stake — but a 10% loss erases it. The multiplier runs both ways. 'Value at Risk' (VaR) tries to cap the danger by estimating the most you'd lose, say, 99 days in 100 — but it says nothing about the 100th day. Long-Term Capital Management (1998) and the 2008 banks were destroyed by leverage meeting a tail event.

media.caption: Leverage steepens the line: bigger gains, and bigger losses.

cards.deploy: Why a 'safe' strategy plus heavy borrowing can still blow up — the anatomy of financial crises.
cards.counter: Nassim Taleb argues VaR is dangerous precisely because it ignores the fat tail beyond its cutoff, breeding false confidence; most firms that blew up in 2008 were inside their VaR limits.

quiz.q: Value at Risk (VaR) is criticised mainly because it…
choices: Ignores the extreme tail beyond its cutoff

cards.title: The mortgage: borrow now, repay for decades
cards.fact: A mortgage spreads a big purchase into level payments — mostly interest at first, mostly principal later.
cards.detail: A mortgage is a loan secured on the property. You repay it in equal instalments, but the split shifts over time. Each payment first covers the interest owed on the outstanding balance; whatever's left chips away at the principal. Early on the balance is huge, so most of the payment is interest; only near the end does it become mostly principal. The level payment on a loan \(P\) at periodic rate \(r\) over \(n\) periods is \(M = P\,\dfrac{r(1+r)^n}{(1+r)^n - 1}\).

media.say: the level payment is the loan times a factor built from the rate and the number of payments.
media.caption: The fixed monthly payment that exactly clears the loan in n periods.
Across a 30-year loan, each payment shifts from mostly interest to mostly principal.

cards.deploy: Explains why early mortgage years build little equity, and why overpaying early saves so much interest.
cards.counter: The level-payment picture assumes a fixed rate; adjustable-rate mortgages reset with market rates, which is how many 2000s borrowers were caught when payments jumped.

quiz.q: In the early years of a standard mortgage, each payment is mostly…

cards.title: Loan-to-value: how leverage swings your equity
cards.fact: Put 10% down and a 10% price move doubles — or wipes out — your stake.
cards.detail: Your equity is the property's value minus the debt. The loan-to-value ratio (LTV) is the debt as a share of value: a 20% deposit means an 80% LTV. Because most of the purchase is borrowed, small price moves swing your equity hugely. Buy a $500k home with $50k down (90% LTV); a 10% price rise ($50k) doubles your equity, while a 10% fall erases it — 'negative equity', where the loan exceeds the home's worth.
cards.deploy: Shows why housing feels so lucrative on the way up and so ruinous on the way down.
cards.counter: Lenders treat the home as collateral, so the downside isn't symmetric for them: in a crash they can force a sale, and in non-recourse US states the owner can walk away — shifting the loss back to the bank.

quiz.q: With a 90% loan-to-value, a 10% fall in the property's price leaves your equity at roughly…

cards.title: NOI and the cap rate: a property's yield
cards.fact: The cap rate is a property's annual income as a percentage of its price — its rental yield.
cards.detail: Net operating income (NOI) is the rent a property earns minus its running costs (maintenance, taxes, insurance), before any mortgage. The capitalisation rate expresses that as a yield: \(\text{Cap rate} = \dfrac{\text{NOI}}{\text{Price}}\). A $1m building with $60k NOI has a 6% cap rate. It's the property world's version of an earnings yield: higher cap rates mean cheaper (or riskier) assets, lower cap rates mean pricier (or safer) ones.

media.say: the cap rate is yearly net income divided by the purchase price.
media.caption: Income as a share of price — a property's yield.

cards.deploy: The quick yardstick investors use to compare income properties and spot over- or under-pricing.
cards.counter: Cap rate ignores financing and growth: it says nothing about your mortgage, future rent rises, or vacancy risk, so two identical cap rates can hide very different deals.

quiz.q: A property earning $60k NOI and priced at $1m has a cap rate of…

cards.title: Three ways to value a property
cards.fact: Appraisers value real estate by comparison, by income, or by replacement cost.
cards.detail: There's no ticker price for a building, so valuers triangulate. The sales-comparison approach looks at what similar nearby properties recently sold for. The income approach capitalises the rent (price = NOI ÷ cap rate) — used for rentals and commercial buildings. The cost approach asks what it would cost to rebuild from scratch, minus depreciation, plus land. Homes lean on comparables; investment property leans on income.
cards.deploy: A framework for sanity-checking any property price: which approach fits, and do they agree?
cards.counter: All three break in thin or frothy markets: comparables vanish when sales dry up, income assumes stable rents, and cost ignores what buyers will actually pay — appraisals lagged badly in both the 2008 bust and the 2021 boom.

quiz.q: Which approach values a rental building from the income it produces?

cards.title: REITs: real estate you can trade like a stock
cards.fact: A REIT pools property into liquid shares that must pay out most of their income.
cards.detail: A real estate investment trust owns income property — malls, flats, warehouses, data centres — and sells shares in it. In exchange for distributing most of their taxable income (in the US, at least 90%) as dividends, REITs largely escape corporate tax. They let small investors hold diversified property without a mortgage or a leaky roof, and they trade on exchanges, so they're far more liquid than a building.
cards.deploy: The accessible way to add real estate to a portfolio — and a daily price signal for the property market.
cards.counter: That liquidity is double-edged: listed REITs trade like equities, so they swing with the stock market in the short run and don't deliver the smooth, uncorrelated returns physical property appears to (partly because buildings just aren't priced every day).

quiz.q: In exchange for tax advantages, REITs must distribute most of their…

cards.title: Why property prices hate rising rates
cards.fact: When interest rates rise, both mortgage affordability and property values fall.
cards.detail: Higher rates hit real estate twice. First, affordability: a buyer's budget is set by the monthly payment they can manage, and higher rates mean a given payment buys a smaller loan — so what people can bid falls. Second, valuation: like a bond, a property is a stream of future income, and a higher discount rate shrinks its present value. Both push prices down, which is why housing markets stall when central banks tighten.

media.caption: As mortgage rates rise, the loan a fixed payment can support (and prices) fall.

cards.deploy: Connects central-bank decisions to your rent, mortgage and house price.
cards.counter: The link is loose and lagged: tight supply, population growth or a strong jobs market can hold prices up despite high rates, as several cities found after 2022.

quiz.q: A rise in interest rates tends to push property prices…

cards.title: Housing bubbles and 2008
cards.fact: Cheap leverage plus the belief that prices only rise is the recipe for a housing crash.
cards.detail: Property bubbles share a pattern: easy credit lets buyers bid with borrowed money, rising prices seem to prove the bet, and lenders relax standards because the collateral keeps appreciating. In the 2000s US, subprime mortgages were bundled into securities rated safe and sold worldwide; when prices turned, the leverage ran in reverse and the losses cascaded into the 2008 crisis. Robert Shiller's Case–Shiller index had flagged the run-up as a bubble; others insisted prices reflected fundamentals.
cards.deploy: A checklist for spotting froth: loosening credit, soaring leverage, and 'prices can't fall' talk.
cards.counter: Calling a bubble in advance is contested: Shiller warned early, but Eugene Fama denies bubbles are even identifiable beforehand, and some economists argue 2008 was a banking-and-leverage failure more than a pure housing-price one.

quiz.q: A common ingredient in housing bubbles is…

cards.title: Taxes: how governments raise money
cards.fact: Governments fund themselves mainly by taxing income, spending, property and profits.
cards.detail: The big revenue sources are income tax, consumption taxes (VAT or sales tax), property taxes, and corporate tax. A system is 'progressive' if higher earners pay a higher share of income, 'flat' if everyone pays the same rate, and 'regressive' if the poor pay a higher share — sales taxes tend to be regressive because the less well-off spend more of their income. How a country mixes these is one of its most consequential political choices.

media.caption: A progressive income tax: higher brackets face higher marginal rates.

cards.deploy: The starting map for any debate about who funds the state and how fairly.
cards.counter: What counts as 'fair' is the live dispute: flat-tax advocates (Hall & Rabushka) prize simplicity and efficiency, while others argue a progressive system is needed to offset widening inequality. Both invoke fairness.

quiz.q: A tax under which lower-income people pay a higher share of their income is…

cards.title: Who really pays a tax?
cards.fact: The party who hands the tax to the government isn't always the one who bears it.
cards.detail: Legal liability and economic burden are different things. A tax lands on whichever side of the market can least easily change its behaviour — the more 'inelastic' side. A tax on cigarettes falls mostly on addicted smokers, who keep buying; a payroll tax 'on employers' is largely passed to workers as lower wages. The seller writes the cheque, but the burden settles where it can't be dodged, regardless of who is legally charged.
cards.deploy: Cuts through political spin: 'we'll tax the corporations' often means workers or customers pay.
cards.counter: Estimating real incidence is hard and contested — economists still argue over how much of corporate tax falls on workers versus shareholders, with credible estimates ranging widely.

quiz.q: The economic burden of a tax falls mainly on the side of the market that is…

cards.title: Deadweight loss and the Laffer curve
cards.fact: Taxes discourage the activity they fall on, so beyond some point higher rates can raise less.
cards.detail: A tax drives a wedge between what buyers pay and sellers receive, so some mutually beneficial trades simply don't happen — that lost value is the 'deadweight loss'. Arthur Laffer dramatised one consequence: a 0% rate raises nothing, and so does a 100% rate (no one works for nothing), so revenue must peak at some rate in between. The shape is real; where the peak sits is the fight.

media.caption: The Laffer curve: 0% and 100% both raise nothing; revenue peaks in between.

cards.deploy: Names the efficiency cost of taxes — and the real question: which side of the peak are we on?
cards.counter: Laffer's curve is used to argue tax cuts 'pay for themselves', but most estimates (and the US Congressional Budget Office) put the revenue-maximising rate far above current top rates, so cuts usually lose revenue. The curve is sound; the political use of it often isn't.

quiz.q: The Laffer curve implies that tax revenue is zero at a rate of…

cards.title: Public goods and the free-rider problem
cards.fact: Some goods everyone can use without using them up — and markets under-supply them.
cards.detail: Paul Samuelson defined a public good by two traits: it's 'non-rival' (my use doesn't reduce yours) and 'non-excludable' (you can't easily stop non-payers). National defence, street lighting and clean air qualify. The snag is the free-rider problem: if you'll benefit whether or not you pay, why pay? So private markets under-provide these goods, which is a core economic justification for taxation and government provision.
cards.deploy: The standard economic case for why some things — defence, basic research, clean air — are funded by the state.
cards.counter: Elinor Ostrom (Nobel 2009) showed communities often manage shared resources themselves without the state, and Ronald Coase argued some 'public goods' (lighthouses) were historically provided privately — so the market-failure case isn't automatic.

quiz.q: A public good is non-rival and…

cards.title: Deficits and debt: a flow and a stock
cards.fact: The deficit is how much a government overspends in a year; the debt is all past deficits piled up.
cards.detail: A deficit is a flow — this year's spending minus this year's revenue. The national debt is the stock — the accumulated total of all past deficits (minus surpluses). Running a deficit adds to the debt, like water flowing into a bath. What matters for sustainability isn't the raw number but the debt-to-GDP ratio: debt measured against the economy's size and ability to service it.
cards.deploy: Stops the common confusion of deficit with debt, and frames debt against the economy's size.
cards.counter: Whether a given debt level is dangerous is fiercely disputed — it hinges on interest rates, growth and whether a country borrows in its own currency, not on any fixed threshold.

quiz.q: The national debt is best described as…

cards.title: Fiscal policy: taxing and spending to steer the economy
cards.fact: Governments can use their budget to cool an overheating economy or revive a slump.
cards.detail: Fiscal policy is the deliberate use of taxes and spending to manage demand. John Maynard Keynes argued that in a downturn the government should spend (or cut taxes) to fill the gap left by frightened households and firms, and that the boost can multiply as the money is re-spent. Against this, advocates of austerity argue that cutting deficits restores confidence and that government borrowing crowds out private investment.
cards.deploy: The framework behind every stimulus-versus-austerity argument after a recession.
cards.counter: The evidence is contested: Keynesians point to the slow recoveries after post-2010 austerity, while Alberto Alesina argued some consolidations were 'expansionary'. A famous prop for austerity — Reinhart & Rogoff's 90%-debt threshold — was undermined when Herndon et al. (2013) found a spreadsheet error.

quiz.q: Keynesian fiscal policy says that in a recession the government should…

cards.title: When is government debt too much?
cards.fact: Debt is sustainable when the economy grows faster than the interest piling up on it.
cards.detail: The debt-to-GDP ratio drifts up or down depending on a race between two rates: the interest rate \(r\) on the debt and the growth rate \(g\) of the economy. Roughly, the change in the ratio is \(\Delta b \approx (r - g)\,b - s\), where \(b\) is debt-to-GDP and \(s\) the primary surplus. If growth outruns interest (\(g > r\)), debt shrinks relative to the economy even while you borrow; if interest outruns growth, debt can spiral.

media.say: the change in the debt ratio is the interest-minus-growth gap times the debt, less the primary surplus.
media.caption: Debt as a share of GDP: the r-versus-g race.

cards.deploy: Reframes 'is the debt too high?' as 'is r below g?' rather than a fixed scary number.
cards.counter: Olivier Blanchard (2019) argued that with r persistently below g, advanced-economy debt is far less alarming than feared; others warn that r can jump suddenly (as in 2022), and that markets can lose confidence well before any formula says so.

quiz.q: Government debt-to-GDP tends to fall over time when…

cards.title: No free lunch: arbitrage
cards.fact: Arbitrage is risk-free profit from a price gap — and the hunt for it forces prices to line up.
cards.detail: If identical cash flows trade at two different prices, you buy the cheap one and sell the dear one for a guaranteed gain. The 'law of one price' says that can't last: arbitrageurs pile in until the gap closes. Almost all modern pricing — Black–Scholes included — assumes no arbitrage exists, which is what pins down a 'fair' price in the first place.
cards.deploy: The bedrock assumption behind every derivative-pricing formula and 'fair value' argument.
cards.counter: Shleifer & Vishny's 'limits of arbitrage' show real arbitrage needs capital and carries risk, so mispricings can persist and even widen — LTCM was an arbitrage that ran out of time before prices converged.

quiz.q: The 'law of one price' says identical cash flows must…

cards.title: The Sharpe ratio: return per unit of risk
cards.fact: Don't compare returns — compare returns divided by the risk taken to get them.
cards.detail: Raw returns flatter risky bets. The Sharpe ratio divides the excess return over the risk-free rate by its volatility: \(S = \dfrac{R - R_f}{\sigma}\). A fund earning 12% at 20% volatility (\(S = 0.5\)) is risk-adjusted-worse than one earning 8% at 8% volatility (\(S \approx 0.75\)). It's the standard way to rank strategies on a level field.

media.say: the Sharpe ratio is the return above the risk-free rate, divided by the volatility.
media.caption: Excess return per unit of risk.

cards.deploy: The headline number for judging whether a return was skill or just leverage and risk.
cards.counter: It treats upside and downside volatility alike and assumes roughly normal returns; a strategy that sells insurance (or options) shows a lovely Sharpe right up until the blow-up. The Sortino ratio penalises only downside to address this.

quiz.q: The Sharpe ratio divides excess return by…

cards.title: The efficient frontier
cards.fact: For every level of risk there's a best-return portfolio — together they trace the efficient frontier.
cards.detail: Markowitz showed that out of all possible portfolios, only those giving the most return for their risk are worth holding — plotted, they form an upward, concave curve: the efficient frontier. Add a risk-free asset and the best trade-off becomes a straight line (the capital market line) touching the frontier at one 'tangency' portfolio. In theory, everyone should hold some blend of cash and that single portfolio.

media.caption: The frontier curves: each extra unit of risk (across) buys less extra return (up).

cards.deploy: The theoretical core of portfolio construction and the case for a single broad market portfolio.
cards.counter: Richard Michaud called it 'error maximization': the frontier is hugely sensitive to the estimated returns and correlations you feed in, so the optimal-looking portfolio is often just fitted to noise.

quiz.q: The efficient frontier shows, for each level of risk, the portfolio with the…

cards.title: Put–call parity
cards.fact: Price a call and the matching put's price is fixed — no-arbitrage locks them together.
cards.detail: Buy a call and sell a put at the same strike \(K\) and expiry, and whatever the price does you end up buying the stock at \(K\) — the same as owning the stock and owing \(K\). No-arbitrage then forces \(C - P = S - K e^{-rt}\). So once you know a call's price, the put's is pinned down, and any gap is free money. It also lets you build 'synthetic' positions from the other pieces.

media.say: a call minus a put equals the stock price minus the discounted strike.
media.caption: No-arbitrage ties calls and puts together.

cards.deploy: A no-arbitrage check on option prices and the recipe for synthetic stock or bonds.
cards.counter: It holds tightly for European options on non-dividend stocks; dividends, early exercise (American options) and borrowing costs open small, real wedges that desks must adjust for.

quiz.q: Put–call parity is enforced by…

cards.title: The yield curve and inversion
cards.fact: Plot bond yields by maturity; when short rates top long rates, recessions often follow.
cards.detail: Normally longer bonds yield more than short ones — an upward-sloping curve — paying you for time and uncertainty. When short-term yields rise above long-term ones, the curve 'inverts': markets are betting growth and rates will fall. An inverted US Treasury curve has preceded every recession since the 1950s, which is why it's among the most watched signals in finance.

media.caption: Maturity (years) across, yield up: an inverted curve slopes down.

cards.deploy: A market-implied recession gauge you can read off the bond market any day.
cards.counter: The timing is loose — a recession can be one to two years out — and some argue quantitative easing and shifting 'term premia' have muddied the signal; 'this time is different' is said before every inversion, occasionally rightly.

quiz.q: An inverted yield curve means short-term yields are…

cards.title: Beyond beta: factor investing
cards.fact: Market risk alone doesn't explain returns — size, value and other factors add to the story.
cards.detail: CAPM uses one factor, the market. Eugene Fama and Kenneth French (1992) showed that small-cap and 'value' (cheap) stocks had beaten what beta alone predicts, and added size and value factors; later models bolted on profitability, investment and momentum. 'Factor' or 'smart-beta' investing tries to harvest these premia systematically rather than picking stocks.
cards.deploy: The modern framework for explaining and engineering returns beyond the single market factor.
cards.counter: John Cochrane warned of a 'factor zoo' — hundreds of published factors, many of which fade out-of-sample or after publication (McLean & Pontiff), hinting at data-mining as much as genuine risk premia.

quiz.q: The Fama–French model added which factors to CAPM's market factor?

cards.title: Debt-service coverage: can the rent pay the loan?
cards.fact: Lenders' first test: does the property's income cover its mortgage, with room to spare?
cards.detail: The debt-service coverage ratio is net operating income divided by the annual loan payment: \(\text{DSCR} = \dfrac{\text{NOI}}{\text{debt service}}\). A DSCR of 1.0 means the rent exactly covers the mortgage; lenders usually want 1.2–1.3 for a cushion. Below 1.0 and the building doesn't pay for itself — the owner must feed it cash each month.

media.say: coverage is the property's net income divided by its yearly loan payment.
media.caption: Above 1.0, the rent more than covers the loan.

cards.deploy: The number that decides how big a loan a property can carry — and an early warning of distress.
cards.counter: DSCR rests on current NOI, which can be flattered by temporary rents or understated expenses; post-2008 lenders learned to stress it against vacancy and rate resets.

quiz.q: A DSCR below 1.0 means the property's income…
choices: Falls short of the loan payment

cards.title: Positive and negative leverage
cards.fact: Borrow below the property's yield and leverage lifts your return; borrow above it and leverage drags.
cards.detail: If a building yields a 7% cap rate and you borrow at 4%, that 3% spread accrues to your smaller slice of equity, magnifying its return — 'positive leverage'. If borrowing costs climb above the cap rate, the same debt now subtracts from your return: 'negative leverage'. The building hasn't changed; the rate environment has. It's why a deal that worked at 4% money can sink at 7%.
cards.deploy: Explains why rising rates quietly turn good property deals bad without any change to the asset.
cards.counter: Positive leverage assumes the cap rate holds; if rents soften or rates rise, the spread can flip overnight, and high leverage then accelerates the loss — the downside of re-ltv-equity.

quiz.q: 'Negative leverage' happens when the borrowing rate is…

cards.title: Mortgage-backed securities and 2008's plumbing
cards.fact: Securitization turns thousands of home loans into tradable bonds — and it sat at the centre of 2008.
cards.detail: Securitization pools mortgages and sells slices ('tranches') of their combined cash flow: senior tranches get paid first and are rated safest, junior ones absorb losses first. It spreads funding and risk — but in the 2000s, pools of subprime loans were sliced into supposedly AAA bonds (RMBS, then CDOs). When defaults hit, those ratings collapsed and the opacity froze global finance.
cards.deploy: The mechanism that connected suburban mortgages to a worldwide banking crisis.
cards.counter: Defenders argue securitization lowers borrowing costs and that the failure was reckless underwriting and conflicted rating agencies, not the structure; the US Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission and Michael Lewis blame the structure for hiding and amplifying the risk. Both readings persist.

quiz.q: A 'tranche' of a mortgage-backed security is…
choices: A slice of the pool's cash flow with its own risk

cards.title: The property cycle: cap-rate compression and expansion
cards.fact: Property values move not only with rents but with cap rates — and cap rates track the rate cycle.
cards.detail: Since price = NOI ÷ cap rate, values can rise two ways: rents grow, or cap rates fall ('compression'). In low-rate booms investors accept ever-lower cap rates, inflating prices even when rents are flat. When rates rise, cap rates 'expand' and prices drop — a repricing that swept commercial real estate in 2022–23 and hit offices hardest.
cards.deploy: Separates the two engines of property value, so you can see when prices are rent-driven or just rate-driven.
cards.counter: Rent moves and cap-rate moves can offset or compound, and the turning points are notoriously hard to time; illiquid private valuations also lag the public signals (REITs) by quarters, masking the turn.

quiz.q: 'Cap-rate compression' pushes property prices…

cards.title: Development: the residual land value
cards.fact: A site is worth whatever's left after building costs and the developer's profit — the residual.
cards.detail: Developers value land backwards: take the finished project's expected value, subtract construction, fees, finance and a required profit margin, and what remains is the most you can pay for the land — its 'residual value'. Because it's a difference of two big numbers, small errors in the end value or costs swing the residual wildly, which is why development is so cyclical and risky.
cards.deploy: The core appraisal for any build: what can I pay for the land and still clear a profit?
cards.counter: The residual is brutally sensitive to assumptions — a 5% slip in sale prices or a cost overrun can erase the entire profit, as many schemes discovered after 2008 and again after 2022.

quiz.q: Residual land value is found by taking the finished value and…

cards.title: Pigouvian taxes: pricing the harm
cards.fact: A Pigouvian tax charges an activity for the harm it does to others — so the price tells the truth.
cards.detail: When an activity dumps costs on others — pollution, congestion — the market overproduces it because the doer doesn't pay. Arthur Pigou's fix: tax it by the size of the external harm, so the private price finally reflects the full social cost and output falls to the efficient level. Carbon taxes are the leading example. Unusually, a well-set Pigouvian tax raises efficiency rather than lowering it.
cards.deploy: The textbook tool for putting a price on pollution and other spillovers.
cards.counter: Ronald Coase argued that with clear property rights and cheap bargaining, the parties can resolve an externality themselves without a tax — and that regulators rarely know the harm precisely enough to set the 'right' rate. Pigou versus Coase is a foundational dispute.

quiz.q: A Pigouvian tax is set equal to the…

cards.title: Inequality: the Gini coefficient
cards.fact: The Gini squeezes a whole income distribution into one inequality number from 0 to 1.
cards.detail: Draw the Lorenz curve: the share of total income held by the poorest \(x\%\) of people. Perfect equality is the 45° line; reality sags below it. The Gini coefficient is the gap between the two, scaled from 0 (everyone equal) to 1 (one person has it all). Tax-and-transfer systems are judged partly by how far they pull the Gini down from its pre-tax level.

media.caption: Gini = the gap between the 45° equality line and the Lorenz curve.

cards.deploy: The standard one-number summary of inequality, and a way to judge redistribution.
cards.counter: One number hides where inequality sits — two countries with the same Gini can differ wildly in their middle and tails — and pre-tax versus post-tax Gini tell very different stories about the same society.

quiz.q: A Gini coefficient of 0 means…

cards.title: The fiscal multiplier
cards.fact: A dollar of government spending can lift output by more — or less — than a dollar.
cards.detail: The fiscal multiplier is the change in GDP per dollar of stimulus. If recipients re-spend it, the dollar circulates and the multiplier tops 1; if it's saved or it crowds out private activity, it's below 1. Crucially, its size depends on the state of the economy: larger in a slump with idle workers and rates near zero, smaller in a boom near capacity.
cards.deploy: The hinge of any stimulus debate: how much GDP do you actually get per dollar spent?
cards.counter: The number is fiercely contested. Blanchard & Leigh (IMF, 2013) found official forecasters had badly underestimated multipliers during post-2010 austerity; Alberto Alesina argued spending multipliers are small. The evidence points to 'it depends on the state of the economy', not a fixed value.

quiz.q: The fiscal multiplier is generally largest when the economy is…
choices: In a deep slump with idle resources

cards.title: Monetary vs fiscal policy
cards.fact: Two levers steer demand: central banks set interest rates; governments tax and spend.
cards.detail: Monetary policy — run by the central bank — adjusts interest rates and the money supply. Fiscal policy — run by the treasury — adjusts taxes and spending. Most rich countries lean on an independent central bank for routine demand management, saving big fiscal moves for deep slumps. Independence is meant to stop politicians from printing money to win elections.
cards.deploy: Sorts out who actually controls what when people argue about 'the government fixing the economy'.
cards.counter: The clean split blurs at the 'zero lower bound', when rates can't fall further and only fiscal policy can act, and when central banks buy government debt (QE) — critics argue that quietly merges the two and erodes independence.

quiz.q: Setting interest rates is the job of…

cards.title: Modern Monetary Theory: the debate
cards.fact: MMT says a country that issues its own currency can't be forced to default — inflation, not solvency, is the real limit.
cards.detail: Modern Monetary Theory (Stephanie Kelton and others) argues a currency-issuing government like the US or UK funds spending by creating money, so it can never simply 'run out'. In this view taxes exist to manage inflation and demand, not to 'pay for' spending. The true constraint is real resources: push spending past the economy's capacity and you get inflation — not bankruptcy.
cards.deploy: A lens that reframes 'how will we pay for it?' as 'will it cause inflation?' for a sovereign currency issuer.
cards.counter: Larry Summers, Kenneth Rogoff and Paul Krugman call MMT dangerously loose: they accept a sovereign issuer can't be forced to default, but argue it understates how hard inflation is to rein back once unleashed — a worry the 2021–23 inflation gave fresh force.

quiz.q: MMT argues the real limit on a currency-issuing government's spending is…

cards.title: Opportunity cost: compared to what?
cards.fact: The real cost of anything is the best alternative you gave up to get it.
cards.detail: Economics starts from scarcity: you can't have everything, so every choice forecloses others. The opportunity cost of an option is the value of the next-best alternative you didn't take — not just the money spent, but the forgone option. An afternoon spent studying costs the leisure or paid work you skipped. Money already spent and unrecoverable (a 'sunk cost'), by contrast, should be ignored when deciding what to do next.
cards.deploy: Forces the honest question behind every choice and policy: compared to what?
cards.counter: The 'next-best alternative' is rarely clear-cut, and people systematically ignore opportunity costs (the neglect documented by Frederick and colleagues), so the principle is easier to state than to live by.

quiz.q: The opportunity cost of a choice is…
choices: The value of the next-best alternative forgone

cards.title: Thinking at the margin
cards.fact: Good decisions weigh the next unit, not the whole — act while the next step still pays.
cards.detail: Economists ask not 'is this worth it?' but 'is one more worth it?'. A choice is optimal when the marginal benefit of the next unit just equals its marginal cost. A firm expands output until the revenue from one more item equals the cost of making it; you keep eating until the next bite's pleasure no longer beats its cost. Reasoning 'at the margin' is the lens behind most of microeconomics.
cards.deploy: Turns a vague 'how much?' into a precise stopping rule: continue while marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost.
cards.counter: Marginal thinking assumes smooth, divisible, well-understood choices; for lumpy, one-off or deeply uncertain decisions it's hard to apply, and people often react to averages or totals instead.

quiz.q: A decision is 'optimal at the margin' when the next unit's…
choices: Marginal benefit equals its marginal cost

cards.title: Diminishing marginal utility
cards.fact: Each extra unit of something usually brings a little less satisfaction than the last.
cards.detail: The first slice of pizza delights; the fifth, less so. This 'diminishing marginal utility' — each additional unit adds less to wellbeing — is why demand curves slope down: you'll only buy more at a lower price. It also grounds the argument that a dollar matters more to a poor person than to a rich one, a key economic case for redistribution.

media.caption: Marginal utility: each extra unit adds less than the one before.

cards.deploy: Explains downward-sloping demand and underpins the efficiency case for redistribution.
cards.counter: Utility can't really be measured in units, and it isn't always diminishing (collectors, addiction); economists now treat it as a convenient ranking of preferences, not a quantity in the head.

quiz.q: Diminishing marginal utility helps explain why demand curves…

cards.title: Elasticity: how much quantity responds to price
cards.fact: Elasticity measures how sharply the quantity bought changes when the price moves.
cards.detail: Price elasticity of demand is the percentage change in quantity divided by the percentage change in price. If a 10% price rise cuts sales by 20%, demand is 'elastic' (elasticity 2) — buyers are price-sensitive. If sales barely move (elasticity below 1), demand is 'inelastic', like petrol or insulin. Elasticity decides who really bears a tax, whether a price cut raises revenue, and how much pricing power a firm has.

media.say: elasticity is the percent change in quantity divided by the percent change in price.
media.caption: Above 1, demand is elastic; below 1, inelastic.
Steep demand = quantity barely moves; flat = very responsive.

cards.deploy: The key to predicting how buyers react to a price change, a tax, or a subsidy.
cards.counter: Elasticity isn't a fixed number — it varies along a demand curve, between the short and long run, and with the substitutes available — so any single figure is a snapshot.

quiz.q: If a price rise barely changes the quantity bought, demand is…

cards.title: Consumer and producer surplus
cards.fact: The gains from trade split into a buyer's surplus and a seller's surplus.
cards.detail: Consumer surplus is the gap between what buyers would have been willing to pay and what they actually pay; producer surplus is the gap between the price sellers receive and the least they'd accept. At the market equilibrium their sum — the total welfare from trading — is as large as it can be. Anything that blocks mutually beneficial trades (a tax, a price cap, a monopoly) shrinks that total: the lost value is the 'deadweight loss'.

media.caption: Supply rises, demand falls; they meet at the price that maximises the gains from trade.

cards.deploy: The yardstick for judging whether a policy makes society better or worse off overall.
cards.counter: Surplus counts dollars, not need: a rich person's willingness to pay can outweigh a poor person's greater need, so 'maximum total surplus' is efficient but not necessarily fair.

quiz.q: Consumer surplus is the gap between what buyers would pay and…

cards.title: Economies (and diseconomies) of scale
cards.fact: Bigger can be cheaper per unit — until it isn't.
cards.detail: As output grows, fixed costs spread over more units and tasks specialise, so the average cost per unit falls — economies of scale. That's how large factories and platforms undercut small rivals. But scale eventually bites back: coordination, bureaucracy and complexity push costs up again (diseconomies of scale), giving the average-cost curve its characteristic U shape, with a 'minimum efficient scale' at the bottom.

media.caption: Average cost per unit: it falls, bottoms out, then rises again.

cards.deploy: Explains why some industries are dominated by giants and others by many small firms.
cards.counter: Where the U bottoms out varies wildly by industry; in software and network businesses near-zero marginal cost can push efficient scale so large that the market tends toward a natural monopoly.

quiz.q: 'Economies of scale' means that as output rises, the cost per unit…

cards.title: Perfect competition: price takers
cards.fact: In perfect competition no single firm sets the price — each just takes it.
cards.detail: The benchmark market: many small firms selling an identical good, free entry and exit, and full information. No one firm can move the price, so each treats it as given and produces up to where price equals marginal cost. Competition then erodes profit to a 'normal' level. Pure perfect competition rarely exists, but it's the yardstick economists hold real, messier markets up against.
cards.deploy: The reference point for judging how much a real market departs from the efficient ideal.
cards.counter: Its assumptions — identical products, perfect information, costless entry — almost never hold; treating it as how markets actually behave, rather than an idealised benchmark, is a common mistake.

quiz.q: A firm in perfect competition is a 'price taker', meaning it…

cards.title: Monopoly: the price maker
cards.fact: A monopolist sets the price — and holds output back to keep it high.
cards.detail: With one seller and no close substitutes, a monopolist faces the whole market's demand curve. To sell more it must cut the price on every unit, so its marginal revenue falls below the price. Producing where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, it deliberately makes less and charges more than a competitive market would — shifting surplus from buyers to itself and creating deadweight loss. This is the core economic case for antitrust law.
cards.deploy: The standard argument for why monopolies are regulated, broken up or blocked.
cards.counter: Some argue monopolies can be efficient (scale, patent-driven innovation) and disciplined by the mere threat of entry; the Chicago school (Robert Bork) narrowed antitrust to consumer prices alone, a stance now challenged by 'neo-Brandeisians' such as Lina Khan.

quiz.q: Compared with perfect competition, a monopoly tends to…

cards.title: Oligopoly and cartels
cards.fact: A few big firms watch each other — and their fates tangle, like a game.
cards.detail: An oligopoly has just a handful of firms, each big enough that its move — a price cut, a new model — affects the others, so all must anticipate rivals' reactions. That makes pricing a strategic game: they'd all profit by colluding to keep prices high, yet each is tempted to undercut and grab share. It's the prisoner's dilemma in the marketplace; cartels like OPEC live this tension.
cards.deploy: Explains why a market with only a few players behaves neither like competition nor pure monopoly.
cards.counter: Whether oligopolists act more like rivals or a hidden cartel is empirical and varies by industry; tacit coordination is hard to prove, which is why competition authorities struggle to police it.

quiz.q: Oligopoly pricing resembles which game?

cards.title: Price discrimination
cards.fact: Charging different buyers different prices for the same thing can raise profit.
cards.detail: A seller with market power who can tell buyers apart by their willingness to pay — and prevent resale — can charge each closer to what they'd bear, capturing surplus that a single price leaves on the table. Airline fares, student and senior discounts, and 'enterprise' software tiers are all price discrimination. It can even expand output, serving customers a single high price would have shut out, so its effect on welfare is genuinely ambiguous.
cards.deploy: Reveals the logic behind coupons, tiered pricing and 'ask for a quote' — and when it helps or harms buyers.
cards.counter: It needs market power and blocked resale, and can feel unfair or shade into exploitation (surge pricing, personalised prices drawn from your data); efficiency and fairness pull in opposite directions.

quiz.q: Price discrimination requires market power and the ability to…

cards.title: Market failure: when markets get it wrong
cards.fact: Even in theory, markets can fail to reach the efficient outcome — the economic case for intervention.
cards.detail: Markets misfire in recognised ways: externalities (costs dumped on third parties), public goods (under-supplied), market power (monopoly), and asymmetric information. Each breaks the link between private incentives and social welfare, leaving room for taxes, regulation or public provision to do better. The list is the standard menu for when 'leave it to the market' has a principled exception.
cards.deploy: A checklist for diagnosing when a market won't fix itself — and what kind of intervention fits.
cards.counter: Spotting a market failure doesn't prove government can do better: public-choice theorists (James Buchanan) and Hayek warn of 'government failure' — capture, poor information, unintended effects — that can be worse than the problem.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a standard source of market failure?

cards.title: Asymmetric information and the market for lemons
cards.fact: When one side of a deal knows more, the market can unravel — Akerlof's 'lemons'.
cards.detail: George Akerlof showed that if sellers know their used cars' quality but buyers don't, buyers will only pay an average price — which drives the good cars out, lowering the average, until the market collapses to 'lemons'. Asymmetric information shapes insurance, credit and labour markets, and the fixes (warranties, credentials, reviews) are everywhere. Akerlof, Michael Spence and Joseph Stiglitz shared the 2001 Nobel for analysing it.
cards.deploy: Explains warranties, certifications, reviews and credentials as cures for a hidden-quality problem.
cards.counter: Signalling and screening can repair the market — Spence showed a credible signal (a costly degree) lets quality reveal itself — so asymmetric information doesn't always destroy trade, and some fixes (runaway credentialism) create new waste.

quiz.q: Akerlof's 'market for lemons' shows that hidden quality can…
choices: Drive good products out of the market

cards.title: Adverse selection
cards.fact: If mainly the high-risk buy insurance, the pool sours before it starts.
cards.detail: Adverse selection is hidden information acting at the moment of sale: those most likely to claim are keenest to buy insurance, so the insurer's pool is riskier than average, which pushes premiums up, which drives out the low-risk — a spiral. It's why insurers screen applicants and why many health systems mandate broad coverage: a compulsory pool stops the healthy opting out and collapsing it.
cards.deploy: The reason insurance is screened, priced by risk, or made compulsory.
cards.counter: Mandates and 'community rating' fight adverse selection but raise their own fairness questions — they force the low-risk to subsidise the high-risk — and where to draw that line is a political choice, not a purely economic one.

quiz.q: Adverse selection in insurance means the buyers most likely to sign up are…

cards.title: Moral hazard
cards.fact: Insure or bail out a risk, and people take more of it.
cards.detail: Moral hazard is hidden action after a deal is struck: once you're insured against a loss you guard against it a little less; once a bank expects a rescue it gambles a little more. The party bearing the consequences can't fully watch the other's behaviour. It framed the fight over 2008's 'too big to fail' bailouts, which arguably rewarded the very recklessness that caused the crisis.
